questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A financial services company runs a trading platform in `us-east4` and connects to its New York data center using two Dedicated Interconnect connections in the same metropolitan area, each in a different edge availability domain. A new regulatory requirement mandates that the hybrid connection be designed to meet Google's highest published availability SLA. The on-premises team can extend circuits to a second colocation facility in another metro. What should the network engineer implement?
options: Add two more Interconnects in the same metro, spread over four availability domains, with one Cloud Router.
Keep the existing topology and add an HA VPN gateway as a backup path over the internet.
Use four Interconnects across two metros, Cloud Routers in two regions and global dynamic routing.
Replace Dedicated Interconnect with Partner Interconnect in two metros using Layer 3 partners overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Google's 99.99% Interconnect topology requires at least four connections across two metros (two edge availability domains per metro), Cloud Routers in two regions, and global dynamic routing so every region can use every path.
questions.distractor_summary: Two connections in one metro, regardless of how many are added there, cap out at the 99.9% topology; an HA VPN backup does not change the Interconnect SLA tier, and switching to Partner Interconnect adds provider dependency without being required.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A healthcare company must let on-premises analytics servers load data into BigQuery and Cloud Storage over its existing Cloud Interconnect. The security team requires that data can never be copied to a Cloud Storage bucket or BigQuery dataset outside the company's organization, even with valid stolen credentials. Traffic must not traverse the public internet. Which design meets these requirements?
options: Use a VPC Service Controls perimeter, restricted.googleapis.com DNS and a 199.36.153.4/30 route advertisement.
Resolve `*.googleapis.com` to `private.googleapis.com`, advertise `199.36.153.8/30` and add IAM deny policies for buckets.
Create egress VPC firewall rules that allow only the Google API IP ranges and deny the rest across the subscriptions.
Put Cloud Armor security policies in front of BigQuery and Cloud Storage to limit which identities call them.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC Service Controls blocks data movement across the perimeter boundary even with valid credentials, and the `restricted.googleapis.com` VIP (`199.36.153.4/30`) only serves VPC-SC-supported APIs so traffic is forced through perimeter enforcement privately over Interconnect.
questions.distractor_summary: The `private.googleapis.com` VIP provides private access but does not enforce the perimeter; firewall rules cannot distinguish buckets owned by different organizations because they share the same API endpoints, and Cloud Armor does not front Google APIs.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: An e-commerce company hosts `shop.example.com` publicly behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Internal batch jobs running on Compute Engine in the production VPC must resolve the same hostname to an internal Application Load Balancer so that traffic stays inside the VPC. External customers must keep receiving the public address. What should you configure in Cloud DNS?
options: Use a DNS forwarding zone for `example.com` that points to an on-premises resolver.
Add a DNS response policy rule on the public zone that returns the internal IP to all clients.
Use one public zone with two A records for `shop.example.com`, one public and one internal.
Add a private zone for `example.com` on the production VPC with an A record to the internal LB.
questions.correct_rationale: Split-horizon DNS is implemented by creating a private zone with the same name as the public zone and authorizing it for the VPC; VMs in that VPC receive the private answer while internet clients continue to query the public zone.
questions.distractor_summary: Two records in one public zone would return the internal IP to internet users as well, a response policy applies to VPC queries rather than creating a dual view, and forwarding to on-premises adds an unnecessary dependency.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A gaming studio is launching a multiplayer backend that uses a custom UDP protocol on port 7777. Game servers run in a regional managed instance group in `europe-west1`. The anti-cheat system requires the original client source IP address to be visible in every packet, and players are almost exclusively in Europe. Which load balancer should you choose?
options: Use an external proxy Network Load Balancer with PROXY protocol enabled for the UDP port.
Use an external passthrough Network Load Balancer with a regional backend service.
Use a global external Application Load Balancer and read the `X-Forwarded-For` header.
Use an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer with Cloud NAT for inbound connections.
questions.correct_rationale: The external passthrough Network Load Balancer supports UDP and does not proxy connections, so backends see the original client source IP in every packet.
questions.distractor_summary: Proxy Network Load Balancers do not support UDP, the Application Load Balancer only handles HTTP(S), and an internal load balancer cannot receive internet traffic (Cloud NAT is outbound-only).

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A media company serves an HTTPS API to users on four continents. Backends run in managed instance groups in `us-central1`, `europe-west4`, and `asia-northeast1`. Leadership wants a single anycast IP address, TLS termination close to the user, and automatic failover to the next-closest region if a regional backend becomes unhealthy. Which design satisfies all requirements?
options: Use a global external Application Load Balancer on Premium Tier with one backend service for all MIGs.
Use three regional external Application Load Balancers on Standard Tier with geolocation DNS routing overall.
Use a global external Application Load Balancer on Standard Tier with Cloud CDN enabled.
Use an external passthrough Network Load Balancer per region with weighted round robin DNS.
questions.correct_rationale: The global external Application Load Balancer provides one anycast IP, terminates TLS at Google Front Ends near users, and spills traffic to the next-closest healthy backend, but it requires Premium Tier.
questions.distractor_summary: Standard Tier does not support global load balancing, and DNS-based designs expose multiple IPs and depend on DNS TTLs rather than health-aware anycast failover.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A regional news publisher in São Paulo serves large video files exclusively to Brazilian viewers from VMs in `southamerica-east1`. The CFO wants to minimize internet egress costs, and the team accepts that traffic may travel over the public internet for more of its path. No global load balancing features are required. What should the network engineer recommend?
options: Keep Premium Tier and enable Cloud CDN on a global external Application Load Balancer overall.
Use Premium Tier with a regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer for the viewers.
Use Standard Tier IP addresses with a regional external load balancer in front of the VMs.
Migrate the content to a multi-region Cloud Storage bucket in `US` with public access overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Standard Tier routes traffic over the public internet closer to the region and has lower egress pricing, which fits a single-region audience that accepts reduced network performance.
questions.distractor_summary: Premium Tier options cost more, Cloud CDN requires a Premium Tier global load balancer, and moving content to a US multi-region would increase latency and still incur egress.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company created a Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL instance with a private IP using Private Service Access in its `prod-vpc`. Applications in `prod-vpc` can connect, but on-premises clients connected via HA VPN to `prod-vpc` time out. The Cloud Router is configured with default route advertisements. What must the engineer do so on-premises clients can reach the database?
options: Create a VPC Network Peering connection between the on-premises network and the producer VPC in every region.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet that hosts the VPN gateway for the instance.
Recreate the instance with a public IP and authorized networks limited to the on-premises range for the team.
Export custom routes on the `servicenetworking` peering and advertise the allocated range via Cloud Router.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Router's default advertisement only includes subnet routes of the VPC, so the PSA allocated range must be added as a custom advertisement, and the peering must export custom routes so the producer VPC learns the on-premises routes for return traffic.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering cannot be established with an on-premises network, Private Google Access concerns Google APIs rather than Cloud SQL private IPs, and a public IP violates the private-connectivity intent.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A retail company runs a Cloud Run service that must call an inventory API hosted on Compute Engine VMs that only have internal IP addresses in `app-vpc`. The platform team wants the lowest latency and the fewest extra resources to manage or pay for, and does not want any intermediary VMs. Which approach should you recommend?
options: Create a Serverless VPC Access connector with at least two instances and route all egress through it.
Configure Direct VPC egress on the Cloud Run service, attached to a subnet in `app-vpc`.
Give the inventory VMs external IPs and allow only Cloud Run's IP ranges in firewall rules.
Publish the inventory API through Private Service Connect and consume it from another VPC.
questions.correct_rationale: Direct VPC egress lets Cloud Run send traffic straight into a VPC subnet without connector instances, giving lower latency and no connector VM costs.
questions.distractor_summary: A Serverless VPC Access connector works but runs billable connector instances that add a hop; external IPs expose the API publicly, and Private Service Connect is unnecessary when both workloads can reach the same VPC.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A SaaS provider hosts a multi-tenant analytics service behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer in its producer VPC (`10.0.0.0/16`). Hundreds of enterprise customers must consume the service privately from their own VPCs. Many customers use `10.0.0.0/16` internally, and the provider must not see or route customer networks. What is the recommended design?
options: Publish with a Private Service Connect service attachment; customers create PSC endpoints in their VPCs.
Peer the VPC with each customer and use custom route exchange to avoid the overlapping ranges.
Build HA VPN tunnels to each customer VPC and filter the overlapping ranges with Cloud Router BGP.
Connect all of the customer VPCs as spokes of a Network Connectivity Center hub with the producer.
questions.correct_rationale: Private Service Connect exposes a producer service through a consumer-side endpoint IP from the consumer's own address space, with NAT on the producer side, so overlapping ranges don't matter and networks are not mutually routed.
questions.distractor_summary: VPC Network Peering and NCC VPC spokes both reject overlapping subnet ranges, and per-customer VPNs don't scale and still require non-overlapping routes.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company uses a Shared VPC with dozens of service projects. Firewall rules currently target network tags, but an audit found that service project developers added the `allow-db-access` tag to unrelated VMs, bypassing segmentation. The security team wants firewall targets whose assignment is controlled through IAM and cannot be applied by anyone with instance-edit permissions. What should the engineer implement?
options: Use service accounts as firewall targets and grant `roles/iam.serviceAccountUser` on all of them.
Keep network tags and use an organization policy to stop tags being added to VMs in the VPC.
Use secure tags bound to the VPC, `tagUser` for approved principals, and network firewall policies.
Move all databases into separate VPCs and connect them with VPC Network Peering between them.
questions.correct_rationale: Secure tags are IAM-governed resources, so only principals granted Tag User on the tag value can bind them, and they are supported as source and target in network firewall policies.
questions.distractor_summary: Granting broad Service Account User recreates the same problem, there is no organization policy that selectively blocks network tags, and splitting VPCs adds complexity without fixing the identity control gap.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A central network team owns the host project of a Shared VPC with subnets in `us-central1` for `payments`, `web`, and `batch` teams. Each team has its own service project. The payments team must be able to deploy VMs only into the `payments-subnet`, and must not be able to use other subnets or modify any network configuration. Which IAM assignment follows least privilege?
options: Grant the payments team `roles/compute.networkUser` at the host project level overall.
Grant the payments team `roles/compute.networkAdmin` on the `payments-subnet` overall.
Grant the payments team `roles/compute.xpnAdmin` at the folder level.
Grant the payments team `roles/compute.networkUser` on the `payments-subnet` only.
questions.correct_rationale: Granting Compute Network User at the subnet level lets service project admins attach resources to that specific subnet only.
questions.distractor_summary: Granting it at the host project level exposes every subnet, Network Admin allows changing network configuration, and Shared VPC Admin (`xpnAdmin`) is for administering the Shared VPC itself.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A manufacturer's on-premises servers need to call Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub, and a Google API that is not supported by VPC Service Controls, all over its existing Dedicated Interconnect. No VPC Service Controls perimeter is planned. Traffic must not use the internet. What should the engineer configure?
options: Resolve `*.googleapis.com` to `restricted.googleapis.com` on-premises, then advertise the `199.36.153.4/30` range.
Resolve `*.googleapis.com` to `private.googleapis.com` on-premises, then advertise the `199.36.153.8/30` range.
Enable Private Google Access on all subnets of the VPC that connects to the Interconnect.
Configure Cloud NAT in the VPC and send the on-premises API traffic through the gateway.
questions.correct_rationale: The `private.googleapis.com` VIP supports most Google APIs regardless of VPC-SC support, and advertising its range through Cloud Router lets on-premises hosts reach it privately over Interconnect.
questions.distractor_summary: The restricted VIP only serves VPC-SC-supported APIs so the unsupported API would fail, the Private Google Access subnet setting applies to VMs in the VPC and not on-premises hosts, and Cloud NAT does not serve traffic originating on-premises.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A bank's on-premises firewall policy only permits outbound connections to RFC 1918 destinations over its Cloud Interconnect. The bank still needs private access to Google APIs from on-premises. The security team also wants API traffic to be addressable with an internal IP they choose. What should the engineer implement?
options: Use a Private Service Connect endpoint for Google APIs with an internal IP, advertised via Cloud Router.
Use a Private Service Access allocation for Google APIs and peer with `servicenetworking.googleapis.com`.
Enable Private Google Access on the subnet of the Interconnect VLAN attachment throughout the organization.
Use an internal Application Load Balancer with an internet NEG that points to `www.googleapis.com` overall.
questions.correct_rationale: A PSC endpoint for Google APIs uses an internal IP you select, so on-premises firewalls only need to allow that RFC 1918 address, and it can be advertised to on-premises with a custom Cloud Router advertisement.
questions.distractor_summary: Private Service Access is for Google-managed producer services such as Cloud SQL, not Google APIs, VLAN attachments have no subnet setting for Private Google Access, and proxying Google APIs through an internet NEG is unsupported and leaves the private path.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A European insurer must ensure that TLS for its customer portal is terminated only within the EU, and that no Google proxy outside the EU ever decrypts traffic. Backends run in `europe-west3`. Customers are all in Germany. Which load balancer design satisfies the requirement?
options: Use a global external Application Load Balancer with backends restricted to `europe-west3`.
Use a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor geo-restriction to EU IPs.
Use a regional external Application Load Balancer in `europe-west3` for the portal.
Use a classic Application Load Balancer with SSL policies that require TLS 1.2.
questions.correct_rationale: A regional external Application Load Balancer terminates TLS on proxies in the region where it is deployed, satisfying data-residency requirements for decryption.
questions.distractor_summary: Global load balancers terminate TLS at Google Front Ends globally near users, which Cloud Armor geo-rules or backend placement cannot prevent, and TLS versions are unrelated to where decryption occurs.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company is designing its landing zone. Production and non-production workloads must be isolated so that a misconfigured firewall rule in development can never affect production, while each environment is still centrally managed by the network team with multiple application service projects. Which VPC design is most appropriate?
options: Use one Shared VPC host project with separate subnets for production and non-production.
Use a standalone VPC for each application, peered together in a full mesh across the company.
Use one Shared VPC with firewall rules that use `prod` and `dev` network tags to isolate them.
Use separate Shared VPC host projects for production and non-production, each with service projects.
questions.correct_rationale: Separate host projects give each environment its own VPC, firewall rule set, and IAM boundary while preserving central network administration through Shared VPC. A single Shared VPC shares firewall and routing scope across environments, so a mistake can cross them; per-application peering meshes don't scale and hit peering limits.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: An organization has three VPCs: `hub`, `spoke-a`, and `spoke-b`. `spoke-a` and `spoke-b` are each peered with `hub`, but workloads in `spoke-a` cannot reach `spoke-b`. The company expects to add 20 more VPCs and wants full-mesh connectivity without managing pairwise peerings. None of the VPCs have overlapping ranges. What should the engineer do?
options: Add a static route in `spoke-a` that points `spoke-b`'s range to the `hub` VPC peering.
Create a Network Connectivity Center hub and add each VPC as a VPC spoke to it.
Enable transitive routing on the `hub` VPC peering connections between the spokes.
Deploy HA VPN between every pair of spoke VPCs in the environment.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC Network Peering is non-transitive, and NCC VPC spokes provide scalable full-mesh (or star) connectivity between many VPCs without pairwise peering.
questions.distractor_summary: Static routes cannot use a peering as a next hop to reach a third VPC, peering has no transitive option, and a VPN mesh grows quadratically in tunnels and cost.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: An engineer attempts to create a VPC Network Peering connection between `vpc-a` (subnet `10.10.0.0/20`) and `vpc-b` (subnet `10.10.8.0/21`). What happens?
options: Peering succeeds, and the more specific `10.10.8.0/21` route wins in both VPCs overall.
Peering succeeds, but only the IPv6 routes are exchanged between the two VPCs overall.
Peering fails because subnet ranges in peered networks cannot overlap each other.
Peering succeeds only if both of the VPCs use global dynamic routing mode.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Cloud prevents peering when subnet IP ranges overlap, because subnet routes are exchanged and must be unique across the peered networks.
questions.distractor_summary: Route specificity does not resolve subnet overlap in peering, and dynamic routing mode affects Cloud Router route propagation, not the peering overlap check.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A large enterprise has exhausted most RFC 1918 space across on-premises and cloud networks. It must deploy several large GKE clusters whose Pod IP ranges are only used inside Google Cloud and never need to be reachable from on-premises. The team wants to avoid using any public address space. Which range should the engineer use for the Pod secondary ranges?
options: Use `100.64.0.0/10` (RFC 6598 shared address space) as non-RFC 1918 private ranges.
Use a routable `/12` owned by another company as privately used public IP space overall.
Use `169.254.0.0/16` link-local space for the workloads in the VPC networks in Azure.
Use `127.0.0.0/8` loopback space for the workloads in the VPC networks in production.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Cloud supports non-RFC 1918 private ranges such as RFC 6598 `100.64.0.0/10` for subnets and secondary ranges, which extends address space without using public IPs.
questions.distractor_summary: Privately used public IPs violate the "no public space" requirement and make the real owners unreachable, while link-local and loopback ranges are not valid subnet ranges.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: To solve address exhaustion, a company configures a GKE subnet secondary range using privately used public IP (PUPI) space `45.20.0.0/16`, which belongs to an external organization. After deployment, developers report that a third-party SaaS API hosted at `45.20.14.10` is unreachable from Pods. What is the cause?
options: Cloud NAT does not support GKE Pods by default, so the traffic is dropped at the edge.
Firewall rules do not allow egress to public IP ranges from the secondary ranges.
PUPI ranges require Premium Tier to reach the external destinations that they use.
Destinations in a PUPI range are treated as internal and routed within the VPC, not to the internet.
questions.correct_rationale: When public space is used privately, the VPC's subnet route for that range takes precedence, so traffic to real internet hosts in that range never leaves the VPC. That is the key tradeoff of PUPI; Cloud NAT can serve GKE, the implied egress allow rule permits the traffic, and network tiers have no bearing on PUPI routing.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A telecom company is enabling IPv6 for a microservices platform. East-west traffic between VMs must use IPv6 without being reachable from the internet, while a separate set of public-facing VMs needs globally routable IPv6 addresses. How should the engineer configure the subnets?
options: Create single-stack IPv6 subnets with external IPv6 ranges and limit them with firewall rules across the subscriptions.
Use ULA internal IPv6 with dual-stack subnets for east-west, and external IPv6 dual-stack subnets for public VMs.
Use IPv4-only subnets and let the load balancer translate IPv6 for all of the traffic throughout the organization overall.
Assign BYOIP IPv6 prefixes to all subnets and filter at the on-premises routers.
questions.correct_rationale: A subnet's IPv6 access type is either internal (ULA, reachable only within the VPC and connected networks) or external (GUA, internet-routable), so separate subnets match each requirement.
questions.distractor_summary: External-only subnets make east-west workloads internet-reachable unless tightly filtered, IPv4-only subnets don't meet native IPv6 requirements, and BYOIP isn't needed for private east-west traffic.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company with an allowlisted public IPv4 `/24` at many partner firewalls is migrating its customer-facing services to Google Cloud and wants to keep using that prefix on Google Cloud load balancers. What is the correct high-level workflow?
options: Create a Public Advertised Prefix with ownership validation, then regional Public Delegated Prefixes.
Create a custom-mode subnet that uses the `/24` as its primary range and assign external IPs from it.
Open a support case to move the prefix into Google's ASN, then reserve static IPs as normal.
Configure Cloud Router to advertise the `/24` from on-premises over Cloud Interconnect to the VPC.
questions.correct_rationale: Bring Your Own IP uses a Public Advertised Prefix (validated via RPKI/ROA and reverse DNS) that is broken into Public Delegated Prefixes from which external addresses are allocated.
questions.distractor_summary: Using the prefix as a subnet range makes it private (PUPI), there is no ASN transfer workflow, and advertising via Interconnect only affects routing toward on-premises.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: After an acquisition, two VPCs that are spokes of a Network Connectivity Center hub each contain a subnet using `192.168.10.0/24`. Workloads in these overlapping subnets must initiate connections to shared services in the other VPC. Readdressing is not possible for 12 months. What should the engineer use?
options: Use VPC Network Peering with custom route import disabled for the overlapping subnets for the application.
Use Cloud NAT with manual external IP allocation in both of the VPCs throughout the organization overall.
Use Private NAT for the overlapping subnets, excluded from NCC exchange, translating to unique ranges.
Use policy-based routes that drop the traffic from the duplicate subnets throughout the organization overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Private NAT translates traffic from overlapping subnets to non-overlapping NAT ranges for VPC-to-VPC communication across NCC spokes, allowing connectivity without readdressing.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering refuses overlapping subnets, public Cloud NAT only handles internet egress, and dropping traffic defeats the requirement.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A team created `app-subnet` as `10.20.0.0/24` in a custom-mode VPC. A regional managed instance group is expected to grow to 700 VMs next quarter. The adjacent range `10.20.1.0/24` is unused, but `10.20.4.0/22` is assigned to another subnet. What is the best action?
options: Shrink the subnet to `/25` and create a second subnet for the remaining VMs for the application.
Add a secondary IP range to `app-subnet` and assign VM primary interfaces from it for the team.
Convert the VPC to auto mode so that it gets larger subnets for the VMs.
Expand `app-subnet` to `10.20.0.0/22` using the gcloud command that expands its IP range.
questions.correct_rationale: A subnet's primary range can be expanded without downtime, and `10.20.0.0/22` (1,020 usable addresses) fits 700 VMs without overlapping `10.20.4.0/22`. Subnet ranges cannot be shrunk, secondary ranges are for alias IPs rather than VM primary interfaces, and a VPC can go from auto to custom mode but not the reverse.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company's security team wants to enforce a baseline across all projects in the organization: deny inbound RDP and SSH from `0.0.0.0/0`, and always allow Google health-check ranges. Project teams must still manage their own application rules but must not be able to override the baseline. What should the engineer implement?
options: Create VPC firewall rules with priority 0 in every VPC, managed by a Terraform pipeline.
Use a hierarchical firewall policy on the organization node with deny and allow rules and `goto_next`.
Use an organization policy constraint that restricts which ports can be opened in projects for the team.
Use global network firewall policies that the project owners attach to each of their VPCs.
questions.correct_rationale: Hierarchical firewall policies at the organization or folder level are evaluated before VPC-level rules, and allow/deny actions there cannot be overridden by project teams, while `goto_next` delegates everything else.
questions.distractor_summary: Priority-0 VPC rules can be modified or deleted by project owners, there is no organization policy constraint that controls firewall ports this way, and network policies attached by project owners aren't centrally enforced.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company routes internet-bound traffic through a pair of third-party firewall appliances fronted by an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer. Only traffic from the `pci-subnet` (`10.50.0.0/24`) must be inspected; all other subnets should keep using the default internet gateway route. How should the engineer steer the traffic?
options: Create a `0.0.0.0/0` static route to the internal load balancer, with a lower priority than default.
Remove the default internet gateway route from the VPC used by the PCI workloads.
Create a policy-based route for source `10.50.0.0/24` with the internal passthrough NLB as next hop.
Apply network tags to the non-PCI VMs and use tag-based static routes for them.
questions.correct_rationale: Policy-based routes can match on source range and steer only that traffic to an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer next hop, leaving other subnets on the default route.
questions.distractor_summary: A lower-priority static route would never be chosen over the default route, removing the default route breaks other subnets, and tag-based routing on non-PCI VMs inverts the requirement and is error-prone.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company runs two next-generation firewall VMs for east-west inspection between subnets. The requirement is automatic failover if the firewall process hangs even though the VM remains running, and traffic for a given flow must return through the same appliance. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use an internal passthrough NLB with health checks as the next hop of custom static routes.
Use two custom static routes with equal priority, each pointing at one firewall VM instance.
Use two static routes with different priorities, each pointing at one firewall VM instance.
Use a regional external Application Load Balancer with the firewall VMs as its backends.
questions.correct_rationale: An internal passthrough load balancer as a route next hop uses health checks to remove failed appliances, and symmetric hashing keeps both directions of a flow on the same backend.
questions.distractor_summary: Next-hop-instance routes are only withdrawn if the VM is stopped or deleted, not when the software hangs, and an external Application Load Balancer cannot serve as a route next hop.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: An engineer wants a single VPC firewall rule whose target is VMs tagged `web` and that also targets VMs running as service account `web-sa@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. What is true?
options: This works, and the rule applies to VMs that match either of the two targets in production.
This works, and the rule applies only to VMs that match both of the two targets by default.
This works only when the rule is defined in a hierarchical firewall policy in every region.
A single VPC firewall rule cannot mix target tags and target service accounts as targets.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC firewall rules can use target network tags or target service accounts, but not both in the same rule.
questions.distractor_summary: Two separate rules are required, and a hierarchical policy does not provide the same mixed-target construct.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company created a development VPC in auto mode and now plans to connect it to its on-premises network, which already uses `10.128.0.0/12` and `10.160.0.0/12`. It also expects to add private regions later. What should the engineer do?
options: Keep auto mode and filter overlapping routes with Cloud Router custom advertisements for the application.
Convert the VPC to custom mode, then create subnets from non-overlapping ranges and migrate workloads.
Delete all auto-created subnets and then switch the VPC to global dynamic routing across the subscriptions.
Use VPC Network Peering with the on-premises network to resolve the overlap.
questions.correct_rationale: Auto mode VPCs create subnets from `10.128.0.0/9` in every region, which overlaps the on-premises ranges, so converting to custom mode and planning non-overlapping ranges is required.
questions.distractor_summary: Route filtering doesn't fix overlapping address assignments, dynamic routing mode doesn't change addressing, and peering can't be established to on-premises networks.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A logistics company cannot reach a Google colocation facility and uses a Layer 2 service provider for Partner Interconnect. The business requires the 99.99% availability SLA. Which configuration should the engineer implement?
options: Use two VLAN attachments in one region, in different availability domains, with one Cloud Router.
Use one VLAN attachment in each of four regions with regional dynamic routing mode.
Use four VLAN attachments in two regions with Cloud Routers in both and global dynamic routing.
Use two VLAN attachments in different metros with HA VPN as a backup path.
questions.correct_rationale: Partner Interconnect's 99.99% topology mirrors Dedicated Interconnect: four VLAN attachments across two regions with redundant edge availability domains, Cloud Routers in each region, and global dynamic routing.
questions.distractor_summary: Two attachments in one region meet only 99.9%, regional routing prevents cross-region failover, and a VPN backup does not upgrade the Interconnect SLA.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A company runs analytics in Google Cloud and transactional systems in AWS. It needs a 10 Gbps private, dedicated connection between a Google Cloud VPC and AWS without procuring colocation space, routers, or cross-connects itself. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Use Cross-Cloud Interconnect with VLAN attachments and Cloud Router BGP sessions to AWS.
Use HA VPN between Google Cloud and an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection for the traffic overall.
Use Partner Interconnect to a carrier that also connects to AWS Direct Connect by default.
Use Direct Peering between the Google and AWS networks for the traffic for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Cross-Cloud Interconnect provides a dedicated physical connection between Google Cloud and another cloud provider, with Google provisioning the connection into the other provider's network.
questions.distractor_summary: HA VPN runs over the internet with lower throughput per tunnel, Partner Interconnect requires a carrier arrangement on both sides, and Direct Peering is for reaching Google's public services, not VPC-to-VPC connectivity.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A startup is replacing an existing Classic VPN, which uses static routes, with a design that supports automatic route updates, a 99.99% SLA, and failover without manual intervention. The on-premises firewall supports BGP and two public IPs. What should the engineer deploy?
options: Use two Classic VPN gateways in different regions with policy-based routing by default.
Use a Classic VPN with route-based tunnels and dynamic routing for the connection overall.
Use a single HA VPN tunnel with static routes configured on both sides.
Use an HA VPN gateway with two tunnels to the peer interfaces and BGP on each tunnel.
questions.correct_rationale: HA VPN offers a 99.99% SLA when both gateway interfaces have tunnels to redundant peer interfaces, and Cloud Router BGP provides dynamic routing and automatic failover.
questions.distractor_summary: Classic VPN has a 99.9% SLA, a single HA VPN tunnel doesn't qualify for 99.99%, and HA VPN requires BGP rather than static routes.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A retailer needs 20 Gbps of private, SLA-backed connectivity from its data center to Google Cloud. The data center is in a city without a Google colocation facility, and the company cannot deploy routers in a colocation facility. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Use Dedicated Interconnect with two 10 Gbps circuits from the data center.
Use Partner Interconnect through a supported provider, with VLAN attachments sized for the bandwidth.
Use HA VPN with four tunnels that are aggregated using ECMP routing.
Use Direct Peering through an internet exchange point close to the data center.
questions.correct_rationale: Partner Interconnect is designed for customers who cannot reach a Google colocation facility, with attachment capacities up to 50 Gbps and SLA-backed topologies.
questions.distractor_summary: Dedicated Interconnect requires meeting Google in a colocation facility, HA VPN runs over the internet with per-tunnel throughput limits, and Direct Peering doesn't provide private VPC access.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A large enterprise's primary Google Cloud usage is Google Workspace and public Google APIs. It wants to reduce internet egress costs and improve performance for this traffic by exchanging routes directly with Google at an internet exchange point. It has no need to reach VPC internal IPs. What should the engineer choose?
options: Use Dedicated Interconnect with VLAN attachments to reach the Google services.
Use Partner Interconnect with a Layer 3 partner to reach the Google services.
Use Direct Peering with Google, which reaches Workspace and the public Google APIs.
Use HA VPN to a VPC that has Private Google Access enabled for the Google services overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Direct Peering establishes BGP sessions with Google's edge network to reach Google's public services, including Workspace, without providing VPC access.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Interconnect is intended for reaching VPC resources, and HA VPN plus Private Google Access routes traffic through a VPC instead of peering at the edge.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A company's Dedicated Interconnect VLAN attachments and Cloud Router are in `us-east4`. New subnets were created in `us-west1` and `europe-west1`, but on-premises routers only learn `us-east4` subnet routes, and on-premises traffic cannot reach the new regions. What is the most likely fix?
options: Change the VPC's dynamic routing mode from regional to global for the Cloud Router.
Create a second VLAN attachment in `us-east4` to carry the traffic of the new subnets.
Add static routes on-premises that point to the new subnets via the Interconnect overall.
Enable Private Google Access on the new subnets in the other regions.
questions.correct_rationale: In regional dynamic routing mode, a Cloud Router only advertises subnets and applies learned routes in its own region; global mode makes subnets in all regions advertised and learned routes usable everywhere.
questions.distractor_summary: Extra attachments in the same region don't change route scope, on-premises static routes don't fix Google-side return routing, and Private Google Access is unrelated.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A retail chain has 300 stores using a third-party SD-WAN solution. It wants the stores to reach workloads in multiple VPCs and to use Google's backbone for store-to-store traffic between regions. The SD-WAN appliances can run as VMs in Google Cloud and speak BGP. What should the engineer design?
options: Use one HA VPN tunnel per store, terminated on the Cloud VPN gateways throughout the organization.
Use Partner Interconnect from each of the stores to reach Google Cloud throughout the organization.
Use Direct Peering from each regional SD-WAN hub to reach Google Cloud throughout the organization.
Register SD-WAN virtual appliances as router appliance spokes on an NCC hub that peers via BGP.
questions.correct_rationale: NCC router appliance spokes let third-party SD-WAN VMs exchange routes with Cloud Router via BGP, and with site-to-site data transfer enabled Google's backbone carries traffic between sites.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-store VPN tunnels and Partner Interconnect at 300 locations are costly and operationally heavy, and Direct Peering doesn't provide VPC access.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A company is planning a hybrid environment spanning on-premises (`10.0.0.0/12`), AWS (`172.16.0.0/16`), and Google Cloud. It expects future acquisitions. What is the best practice for Google Cloud address planning?
options: Use auto mode VPCs so that the ranges are chosen automatically for the workloads.
Allocate a non-overlapping supernet from a central IPAM plan and reserve space for GKE and PSA ranges.
Reuse `10.0.0.0/12` in Google Cloud and rely on Cloud NAT for the translation.
Use `172.16.0.0/16` in Google Cloud since the AWS traffic will be routed separately.
questions.correct_rationale: A centralized IPAM plan with a dedicated non-overlapping supernet, including room for GKE secondary ranges and Private Service Access allocations, prevents routing conflicts across hybrid and multicloud networks.
questions.distractor_summary: Auto mode ranges are fixed and may overlap on-premises space, and reusing existing ranges breaks routing since Cloud NAT only handles internet egress.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A company created a Cloud DNS outbound forwarding zone for `corp.example.com` targeting on-premises DNS servers at `10.1.1.53` and `10.1.1.54`. The HA VPN tunnels are up, and VMs can ping the DNS servers, but DNS queries from VMs for `corp.example.com` time out. What is the most likely cause?
options: Private Google Access is disabled on the subnets of the VMs that query the zone for the application.
The forwarding zone must use public IP addresses as its targets for DNS queries.
The on-premises network has no return route to `35.199.192.0/19`; advertise it from Cloud Router.
Cloud DNS forwarding requires Cloud NAT before it can reach on-premises name servers in production.
questions.correct_rationale: Forwarded queries to private targets originate from `35.199.192.0/19`, so on-premises networks need a route for that range back through the VPN, typically via a Cloud Router custom advertisement.
questions.distractor_summary: Private Google Access and Cloud NAT are unrelated to forwarding, and forwarding zones support private RFC 1918 targets.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: On-premises applications must resolve records in Cloud DNS private zones authorized for `prod-vpc`, which connects to on-premises via Cloud Interconnect. What should the engineer configure?
options: Create an inbound DNS server policy on `prod-vpc` and forward the zones from on-premises to its IPs.
Create an outbound forwarding zone for the private zones that points to the on-premises DNS as needed.
Make the zones public and restrict access to them with firewall rules.
Create a DNS peering zone from the on-premises network to `prod-vpc`.
questions.correct_rationale: An inbound server policy creates entry-point IPs in the VPC's subnets that on-premises resolvers can forward to over hybrid connectivity to resolve private zones.
questions.distractor_summary: Outbound forwarding goes the other direction, public zones expose internal records, and DNS peering only works between VPC networks.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A company has a `dns-hub` VPC with Interconnect to on-premises and outbound forwarding zones for `corp.example.com`. Fifteen workload VPCs, not peered with `dns-hub` and not connected to on-premises, must resolve `corp.example.com` through the same path. What is the most scalable design?
options: Duplicate the outbound forwarding zones in each of the workload VPCs across the subscriptions.
Deploy BIND servers in each of the workload VPCs to forward the queries on for the application.
Configure an inbound server policy in each of the workload VPCs for the zone in every region.
Create DNS peering zones in each workload VPC that target `dns-hub` for `corp.example.com`.
questions.correct_rationale: DNS peering lets a VPC send queries for a zone to another VPC's resolution order, so the hub's forwarding zones serve every workload VPC without network connectivity to on-premises.
questions.distractor_summary: Duplicated forwarding zones in unconnected VPCs cannot reach on-premises servers, self-managed BIND adds operational overhead, and inbound policies handle queries entering from outside.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A payment processor uses Partner Interconnect. A new PCI DSS interpretation requires all traffic between the data center and Google Cloud to be encrypted with IPsec. The company wants to keep the Interconnect's private bandwidth. What should the engineer implement?
options: Enable MACsec on the Partner Interconnect VLAN attachments to encrypt the traffic overall.
Deploy HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect, using encrypted VLAN attachments for the traffic.
Replace Partner Interconnect with HA VPN over the internet for the encrypted traffic overall.
Enable TLS on every application and keep the Interconnect itself unencrypted.
questions.correct_rationale: HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect runs IPsec tunnels across encrypted VLAN attachments, keeping private connectivity while satisfying an IPsec requirement.
questions.distractor_summary: MACsec is available for Dedicated and Cross-Cloud Interconnect, not Partner Interconnect, moving to internet VPN sacrifices the private path, and application TLS doesn't satisfy a network-layer IPsec mandate.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A company wants to improve internet performance to Google Cloud services for branch offices but cannot justify Direct Peering or Interconnect. Its regional ISP is listed in Google's Verified Peering Provider program. What does using this ISP provide?
options: Provide private RFC 1918 access to the VPC resources through the ISP.
Provide an SLA-backed 99.99% dedicated connection to Google Cloud for the offices overall.
Provide redundant internet paths to Google's edge, without peering directly with Google.
Provide automatic encryption of all traffic to the Google APIs from the offices.
questions.correct_rationale: Verified Peering Providers are ISPs that meet Google's peering and redundancy criteria, improving access to Google's public services over the internet.
questions.distractor_summary: They don't provide private VPC access or Interconnect SLAs, and they don't add encryption.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.subdomain: 1.3 Design resilient hybrid and multicloud connectivity
questions.question: A company connects Google Cloud to Microsoft Azure using HA VPN. The Azure VPN gateway is active-active with two public IPs. The company wants Google's 99.99% HA VPN SLA. How should the connection be configured?
options: Use an HA VPN gateway, an external gateway with two interfaces, four tunnels and BGP on each.
Use a Classic VPN gateway with two tunnels to the two Azure IP addresses.
Use an HA VPN gateway with one tunnel to one Azure IP and a static route backup.
Use Cross-Cloud Interconnect with a single VLAN attachment between the clouds.
questions.correct_rationale: For a peer with two interfaces, Google's recommended HA VPN topology uses a two-interface external VPN gateway and four tunnels with BGP to achieve the 99.99% SLA. Classic VPN is limited to 99.9%, a single tunnel doesn't qualify for 99.99%, and a single VLAN attachment lacks redundancy.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A production GKE cluster has exhausted its Pod secondary range, so new nodes fail to be created. The cluster must keep running, and the existing range cannot be expanded because adjacent space is used. What should the engineer do?
options: Recreate the cluster with a larger Pod range and migrate the workloads to it overall.
Change the cluster's Service range to a larger block of addresses for the Pods.
Add a new secondary range to the subnet and use it for a new node pool's Pods.
Increase the maximum Pods per node on the existing node pools of the cluster overall.
questions.correct_rationale: GKE supports discontiguous multi-Pod CIDR, allowing new node pools to use additional Pod ranges without recreating the cluster.
questions.distractor_summary: Recreating the cluster is disruptive, the Service range doesn't provide Pod addresses, and raising max Pods per node increases per-node block size and consumes the range faster.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: When planning a GKE cluster's Service (ClusterIP) range in a VPC-native cluster connected to on-premises, which statement is correct?
options: Keep the Service range unique, with no overlap of subnets, secondary ranges or on-premises ranges.
The Service range can overlap on-premises ranges because ClusterIPs are never routed outside overall.
The Service range must be a public range so that it supports external load balancers in every region.
The Service range is automatically expanded by GKE when it becomes exhausted.
questions.correct_rationale: Best practice is to allocate the Service range from non-overlapping space so traffic to on-premises or peered destinations in that range isn't intercepted by cluster Service routing.
questions.distractor_summary: ClusterIPs are internal, so the range doesn't need to be public, and GKE does not automatically expand the Service range.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A security team requires that GKE nodes have no external IP addresses, and that the Kubernetes control plane be reachable only from the corporate office's public egress range `203.0.113.0/24` and from the VPC. Developers use kubectl from the office. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use public nodes with a firewall rule that restricts SSH to `203.0.113.0/24`.
Use private nodes with the control plane's public endpoint disabled entirely.
Use private nodes with no authorized networks configured on the control plane for the application.
Use private nodes with the public endpoint on and authorized networks set to `203.0.113.0/24`.
questions.correct_rationale: Private nodes remove external IPs, and authorized networks restrict public-endpoint access to the office range while VPC access uses the private endpoint.
questions.distractor_summary: Public nodes violate the no-external-IP requirement, disabling the public endpoint blocks office kubectl without a hybrid path, and no authorized networks leaves the public endpoint open.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A service project team wants to create a GKE cluster in a Shared VPC subnet owned by the host project. Cluster creation fails with permission errors on the subnet. Secondary ranges for Pods and Services already exist on the subnet. What must be granted?
options: Grant `roles/container.admin` on the host project to the service project developers.
Grant `compute.networkUser` on the subnet and `container.hostServiceAgentUser` on the host project.
Grant `roles/compute.xpnAdmin` to the GKE service agent of the service project.
Grant `roles/owner` on the host project to the Compute Engine default service account.
questions.correct_rationale: GKE in Shared VPC requires the service project's GKE and Google APIs service agents to have Network User on the subnet, and the GKE service agent needs Host Service Agent User on the host project to manage firewall resources.
questions.distractor_summary: The other options grant broad or unrelated roles and violate least privilege.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: A company is migrating to GKE Autopilot and asks whether it can install Calico to enforce Kubernetes NetworkPolicy, as it did on self-managed clusters. What should the engineer tell them?
options: Autopilot supports Calico when it is enabled at cluster creation time.
Autopilot does not support NetworkPolicy, so firewall rules are used instead in every region.
Autopilot uses GKE Dataplane V2 to enforce NetworkPolicy natively, so Calico is not needed.
Autopilot requires Istio sidecars to be injected before NetworkPolicy is enforced by default.
questions.correct_rationale: Autopilot clusters use GKE Dataplane V2 (eBPF-based), which enforces NetworkPolicy natively, and users can't install their own CNI. NetworkPolicy is supported, VPC firewall rules don't provide Pod-level policy, and a service mesh isn't required.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: Pods in a VPC-native GKE cluster must connect to an on-premises database at `10.200.5.20` over Cloud Interconnect. The on-premises firewall only allows the node subnet range, not the Pod range, and security won't change it. Connections from Pods are dropped. What should the engineer do?
options: Configure Cloud NAT for the Pod range so that the traffic leaves the cluster throughout the organization overall.
Advertise the Pod range to the on-premises network through Cloud Router and BGP.
Recreate the cluster as a routes-based cluster so that Pod traffic is masqueraded across the subscriptions.
Set the ip-masq-agent so on-premises is not in `nonMasqueradeCIDRs`, SNATing Pod traffic to the node IP.
questions.correct_rationale: By default, GKE doesn't masquerade traffic to RFC 1918 destinations, so on-premises sees Pod IPs; customizing ip-masq-agent to exclude the on-premises range makes that traffic use the node IP the firewall allows.
questions.distractor_summary: Public Cloud NAT handles internet egress, advertising Pod ranges doesn't satisfy the firewall constraint, and routes-based clusters are legacy and still use Pod IPs.

questions.domain: 1. Designing and Planning a Google Cloud Network
questions.question: Administrators need to run kubectl from on-premises against a GKE cluster whose control plane has only a private endpoint enabled. The on-premises network connects to the cluster's VPC via HA VPN. Commands time out. What should the engineer do?
options: Enable the public endpoint without any authorized networks for the administrators across the subscriptions.
Add the on-premises range to authorized networks and advertise the control-plane range via Cloud Router.
Create a Cloud NAT gateway for the control plane range so kubectl can reach it.
Enable Private Google Access on the node subnet so that kubectl can connect.
questions.correct_rationale: Reaching a private control-plane endpoint from on-premises requires authorized networks to include the on-premises range and a routable path, which means advertising the endpoint range and, for peering-based control planes, exporting routes so return traffic works.
questions.distractor_summary: Enabling an open public endpoint weakens security, Cloud NAT doesn't provide inbound reachability, and Private Google Access doesn't reach the control plane.

questions.question: A data engineering team runs Dataproc clusters on VMs without external IP addresses. Clusters in `subnet-a` can read from Cloud Storage, but identical clusters in `subnet-b` of the same VPC and region fail with connection timeouts to `storage.googleapis.com`. Both subnets use the same firewall rules and the VPC still has its default internet gateway route. What is the most likely fix?
options: Assign external IP addresses to the VMs in `subnet-b` so they can reach the APIs.
Create a Cloud NAT gateway for `subnet-b` only, to reach the Google APIs.
Enable Private Google Access on `subnet-b` so the VMs can reach the Google APIs.
Create a VPC Network Peering connection to `servicenetworking.googleapis.com` for the VMs.
questions.correct_rationale: Private Google Access is configured per subnet, and it lets VMs with only internal IPs reach Google APIs through the default internet gateway route.
questions.distractor_summary: External IPs or Cloud NAT would also work but add public exposure or cost that isn't required, and the `servicenetworking` peering is for Private Service Access to managed services like Cloud SQL, not Google APIs.

questions.question: To prevent any direct internet egress, a security team deleted the `0.0.0.0/0` default internet gateway route from a production VPC. Private Google Access remains enabled on all subnets, but workloads can no longer reach Cloud Storage or BigQuery. The team wants API access restored without re-enabling general internet egress. What should the engineer do?
options: Map `*.googleapis.com` to `private.googleapis.com` and add a `199.36.153.8/30` route to the default gateway.
Re-create the `0.0.0.0/0` route at priority 65535 so it is only used as a last resort.
Deploy Cloud NAT and restrict it to the Google API ranges for the private VMs.
Disable and re-enable Private Google Access on each subnet to refresh the routing.
questions.correct_rationale: Private Google Access still requires a route to Google API addresses via the default internet gateway, so pointing DNS at the `private.googleapis.com` VIP and adding a route for only `199.36.153.8/30` restores API access without a general internet path.
questions.distractor_summary: A low-priority default route still provides internet egress, Cloud NAT can't filter by destination, and toggling the setting doesn't create the missing route.

questions.question: A network engineer has the Owner role on both a new network project and three application projects. When the engineer tries to enable the network project as a Shared VPC host project, the operation fails with a permission error. What does the engineer need?
options: Hold `roles/compute.networkAdmin` on the network project, in addition to the Owner role overall.
Hold the Organization Administrator role on the organization itself.
Hold `roles/compute.networkUser` on each of the application projects throughout the organization.
Hold the Shared VPC Admin role (`roles/compute.xpnAdmin`) at the organization or folder level.
questions.correct_rationale: Enabling a host project and attaching service projects requires the Shared VPC Admin role granted at the organization or folder level containing the projects.
questions.distractor_summary: Project Owner and Network Admin are project-scoped and don't include Shared VPC administration, Network User is for consuming subnets, and Organization Administrator manages IAM but isn't itself the Shared VPC permission.

questions.question: A company adopts Shared VPC. The finance team asks where costs for VMs in service projects will be billed, and the security team asks where firewall rules protecting those VMs will be created and managed. What is the correct answer?
options: VM costs are billed to the host project, and firewall rules are created in each service project for the team.
VM costs are billed to the service project; firewall rules for the shared network are in the host project.
VM costs and firewall rules are both in the host project of the Shared VPC.
VM costs and firewall rules are both in the service project that owns the VMs.
questions.correct_rationale: Resources such as VMs belong to and are billed to the service project in which they are created, while the network itself, including its firewall rules and routes, lives in the host project.
questions.distractor_summary: This separation lets application teams own costs while the network team retains control of network policy.

questions.question: `vpc-a` and `vpc-b` are peered, and `vpc-a` exports custom routes while `vpc-b` imports them. In `vpc-a`, a static route for `172.20.0.0/16` points to a NAT VM and applies only to VMs with the network tag `legacy`. Engineers notice the route never appears in `vpc-b`. What is the reason?
options: Static routes are never exported over VPC Network Peering to the peer network overall.
Custom route import requires global dynamic routing on `vpc-b` before it takes effect.
Static routes that use network tags are not exchanged over VPC Network Peering.
The route's destination overlaps a subnet that already exists in `vpc-b` overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom static routes can be exchanged over peering when export and import are enabled, but routes scoped with network tags are never exchanged.
questions.distractor_summary: Dynamic routing mode affects Cloud Router routes rather than peering import, and an overlap would produce a different error or conflict than a silently missing tagged route.

questions.question: `vpc-a` uses a subnet with a privately used public IPv4 (PUPI) range, `52.10.0.0/20`, for batch VMs. `vpc-a` is peered with `vpc-b`, and all other subnets are reachable from `vpc-b`, but the PUPI subnet is not present in `vpc-b`'s routing table. What should the engineer configure?
options: Enable importing subnet routes with public IPs on `vpc-b`'s side of the peering.
Enable custom route export on `vpc-a` and custom route import on `vpc-b` together.
Create a static route in `vpc-b` for `52.10.0.0/20` with the peering as next hop.
Re-create the subnet from an RFC 1918 range because PUPI subnets cannot be peered.
questions.correct_rationale: By default, a network exports its PUPI subnet routes, but the peer does not import them until import of subnet routes with public IPs is enabled on its side.
questions.distractor_summary: Custom route settings apply to static and dynamic routes rather than subnet routes, peering can't be a static route next hop, and PUPI subnets can be peered.

questions.question: A team created a new custom-mode VPC and deployed VMs with no external IPs. Admins must SSH using Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding. The IAM `roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor` role is granted, but connections fail. No firewall rules exist yet. What should the engineer add?
options: Allow an egress rule for TCP 22 to `0.0.0.0/0` from the VMs.
Allow an ingress rule for TCP 22 from `35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22`.
Create a Cloud NAT gateway so that IAP can reach the VMs without external IPs.
Allow an ingress rule for TCP 22 from `35.235.240.0/20` to the target VMs.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom-mode VPCs have only the implied deny-ingress rule, so an ingress rule must allow TCP 22 from IAP's forwarding range `35.235.240.0/20`. Egress is already allowed by the implied rule, the other ranges are for load balancer health checks, and Cloud NAT only handles outbound traffic.

questions.question: A company uses Private Service Access for Cloud SQL and Memorystore with an allocated range of `10.100.0.0/24`. Creating new Cloud SQL instances in another region now fails with an error indicating insufficient IP space in the allocated range. What should the engineer do?
options: Expand the allocated range to `/20` using the subnet expand command for the range for the application.
Allocate an additional range for Private Service Access and update the connection with both ranges.
Delete the private connection and recreate it with a larger allocated range.
Create the new instances with a public IP address only, without private access.
questions.correct_rationale: You can add allocated ranges to an existing private services connection by updating it with the full list of ranges, without disrupting existing instances.
questions.distractor_summary: Allocated ranges aren't subnets and can't be expanded with the subnet command, deleting the connection disrupts existing services, and public IP contradicts the private design.

questions.question: An engineer is deploying a regional internal Application Load Balancer in `us-central1` to front microservices in a Shared VPC. Creating the forwarding rule fails with an error indicating that a required subnet is missing. What must be created?
options: Add a second subnet with Private Google Access enabled in the region.
Add a Private Service Connect subnet in the region for the load balancer throughout the organization.
Create a proxy-only subnet in `us-central1` with purpose `REGIONAL_MANAGED_PROXY`, role `ACTIVE`.
Add a subnet with a secondary range reserved for the load balancer VIPs throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: Envoy-based regional load balancers, including the internal Application Load Balancer, require a proxy-only subnet in the region and VPC from which the proxies source traffic to backends.
questions.distractor_summary: Private Google Access isn't related, PSC subnets are for producer NAT, and VIPs come from a regular subnet rather than a secondary range.

questions.question: A VPC has a dynamic route for `10.0.0.0/8` learned from on-premises through Cloud Router with priority 100, and a custom static route for `10.1.0.0/16` pointing to a firewall appliance with priority 1000. A VM sends a packet to `10.1.5.20`. Which route is used?
options: The static `10.1.0.0/16` route wins, because the most specific destination is chosen before priority.
The dynamic `10.0.0.0/8` route wins, because it has the lower priority value throughout the organization.
Both routes are used by the VPC, with traffic split across them using ECMP throughout the organization.
The dynamic route wins, because dynamic routes always take precedence over static routes in production.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Cloud route selection first chooses the longest prefix match, and priority only breaks ties between routes with the same destination prefix.
questions.distractor_summary: ECMP applies only to equal prefixes and priorities, and dynamic routes don't automatically take precedence over static routes.

questions.question: A company operates three self-managed NAT VMs for a legacy application that requires specific source IPs. The engineer wants outbound traffic from tagged application VMs to be distributed across all three NAT VMs. How should the routes be configured?
options: Use three static routes for `0.0.0.0/0` with priorities 800, 900 and 1000, one per NAT VM.
Use three static `0.0.0.0/0` routes with equal priority and one tag, each with a different NAT VM.
Use one static route that points to a managed instance group of the NAT VMs.
Use a policy-based route that has three next hops, one for each of the NAT VMs.
questions.correct_rationale: When multiple routes share the same destination and priority, Google Cloud uses equal-cost multipath (ECMP) to spread flows across the next hops.
questions.distractor_summary: Different priorities create active/standby behavior rather than distribution, an instance group isn't a valid static route next hop, and policy-based routes take a single next hop.

questions.question: A VPC in global dynamic routing mode has Cloud Routers in `us-east4` and `us-west1`, each receiving `192.168.0.0/16` from on-premises with the same MED over separate Interconnects. VMs in `us-west1` send traffic through the `us-west1` Interconnect, and VMs in `us-east4` use the `us-east4` Interconnect. Why?
options: Regional subnets can only use the Cloud Routers that are in their own region.
The on-premises routers are sending different AS paths to each of the regions for the application.
Cloud Router always prefers the most recently learned route among those it has for the application.
In global mode, routes learned in another region get an inter-region cost, so local routes win.
questions.correct_rationale: With global dynamic routing, Google Cloud adds a region-to-region cost to the base priority of routes learned in other regions, so VMs prefer same-region paths when MEDs are equal.
questions.distractor_summary: In global mode, subnets can use Cloud Routers in any region, the scenario states identical advertisements, and Cloud Router doesn't prefer routes based on recency.

questions.question: A company is migrating a legacy application whose VMs must send all internet traffic through an explicit proxy VM for compliance, while other VMs in the same subnet should continue using the default internet gateway. The legacy VMs are tagged `legacy-app`. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a policy-based route that matches the subnet's source range with the proxy VM as next hop.
Delete the default route and add a `0.0.0.0/0` route to the proxy VM for everyone.
Add a `0.0.0.0/0` static route to the proxy VM, tagged `legacy-app`, with priority 900.
Add a `0.0.0.0/0` static route to the proxy VM with the priority set to 1100.
questions.correct_rationale: Tag-scoped static routes apply only to VMs with that tag, and priority 900 beats the default internet gateway route's priority of 1000 for those VMs.
questions.distractor_summary: A source-range policy-based route would capture every VM in the subnet, removing the default route affects all VMs, and priority 1100 loses to the default route.

questions.question: An on-premises team begins advertising `0.0.0.0/0` to Google Cloud over Cloud Interconnect with a MED of 100. The VPC still has the default internet gateway route with priority 1000. What happens to internet-bound traffic from VMs?
options: It goes to on-premises over the Interconnect, since the learned default route has a better priority.
It keeps using the default internet gateway, since system-generated routes cannot be overridden overall.
It is load-balanced between the two routes using ECMP routing across both of them for the application.
It is dropped, because the two default routes conflict with each other for the VPC for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Both routes have the same prefix, so priority decides, and the learned route's priority of 100 beats the default route's 1000, forcing internet traffic on-premises.
questions.distractor_summary: The default internet gateway route is a custom-editable route, ECMP applies only to equal priorities, and conflicting routes are resolved by priority rather than dropped.

questions.question: An engineer created a policy-based route that sends all traffic from `app-subnet` (`10.30.0.0/24`) to an internal passthrough load balancer fronting inspection appliances. Afterward, traffic between VMs within the VPC's own internal ranges (`10.0.0.0/8`) is also being sent through the appliances, adding latency. Internal traffic must bypass inspection. What should the engineer do?
options: Delete the policy-based route and use tagged static routes instead for the subnet for the application.
Lower the priority of the subnet routes of the VPC so that they are used less.
Add firewall rules that deny traffic to the appliances from the internal ranges for the application.
Add a higher-priority policy-based route for `10.30.0.0/24` to `10.0.0.0/8` with default routing.
questions.correct_rationale: Policy-based routes are evaluated before other routes, and a higher-priority PBR that sends matching traffic to default routing (`--next-hop-other-routes=DEFAULT_ROUTING`) makes internal flows bypass the appliance.
questions.distractor_summary: Tagged routes don't provide source-based steering for the whole subnet, subnet route priorities can't be changed, and firewall denies would break the traffic.

questions.question: A company has 180 subnets within `10.20.0.0/16` in Google Cloud. The on-premises edge router has a limit on accepted prefixes and has begun rejecting routes. The network team wants on-premises to receive a single summary route. What should the engineer configure on Cloud Router?
options: Change the VPC to regional dynamic routing mode for the Cloud Router advertisements for the team.
Use custom advertisement mode, drop the all-subnets advertisement and advertise `10.20.0.0/16`.
Enable BGP route aggregation on the VLAN attachments for the on-premises routers.
Configure custom learned routes for `10.20.0.0/16` on the Cloud Router.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom advertisement mode lets Cloud Router advertise user-defined prefixes, such as a single summary, instead of every individual subnet.
questions.distractor_summary: Regional mode only limits which regions are advertised, VLAN attachments have no aggregation setting, and custom learned routes affect routes received into the VPC.

questions.question: A partner's legacy router establishes a BGP session with Cloud Router but can't advertise the partner's `198.51.100.0/24` range due to a software limitation. The VPC must still route traffic for that range to the partner over this BGP session, and the route should be withdrawn automatically if the BGP session goes down. What should the engineer use?
options: Add a static route for `198.51.100.0/24` with the VLAN attachment as the next hop.
Add a policy-based route for the destination with the Cloud Router as the next hop.
Configure custom learned routes on the Cloud Router BGP peer for `198.51.100.0/24`.
Configure a custom route advertisement for `198.51.100.0/24` on Cloud Router.
questions.correct_rationale: Custom learned routes make Cloud Router install routes as if they were received from the BGP peer, and those routes are withdrawn when the session goes down.
questions.distractor_summary: VLAN attachments and Cloud Routers aren't valid next hops for static or policy-based routes, and custom advertisements send routes to the peer rather than learning them.

questions.question: To test an isolated environment, an engineer deletes the default internet gateway route from a VPC that hosts backends for a global external Application Load Balancer. The load balancer continues to serve traffic and health checks keep passing. Why?
options: Health check and Google Front End traffic uses special return paths that do not depend on routes.
Deleting the default route only takes effect after the VMs are restarted throughout the organization.
Load balancers create hidden `0.0.0.0/0` routes for their backends in the VPC across the subscriptions.
Health checks run from inside the subnets of the VPC rather than from Google across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Cloud uses special routing paths for responses to health checkers and Google Front Ends, so these flows work without a default internet gateway route.
questions.distractor_summary: Route changes apply immediately, load balancers don't add hidden default routes, and health checks originate from Google ranges such as `35.191.0.0/16` and `130.211.0.0/22` rather than from customer subnets.

questions.question: A company has one shared-services VPC and 12 development VPCs, all non-overlapping. Every development VPC must reach the shared-services VPC, but development VPCs must never reach each other. The team wants a managed solution without writing firewall rules to block inter-dev traffic. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use an NCC hub in mesh topology with all of the VPCs added as spokes.
Use VPC Network Peering from each dev VPC to shared services, plus deny firewall rules in Azure.
Use Shared VPC with each development team as a service project of the host across the subscriptions.
Use an NCC star hub with shared services in the center group and development VPCs on the edge.
questions.correct_rationale: NCC star topology lets edge spokes reach center spokes while preventing edge-to-edge connectivity, matching the isolation requirement without firewall rules.
questions.distractor_summary: Mesh topology connects all spokes, peering doesn't provide isolation on its own (it's non-transitive but needs a separate design for scale), and Shared VPC places everything in a single network.

questions.question: A VPC that is an NCC VPC spoke contains a subnet `10.99.0.0/24` used for a sensitive management network. Other spokes must not learn routes to it, while the rest of the VPC's subnets must remain reachable. What should the engineer configure?
options: Add an egress deny firewall rule in each of the other spokes on the hub as needed.
Add an export filter on the VPC spoke that excludes `10.99.0.0/24` from the hub.
Move the subnet to regional dynamic routing mode for the VPC spoke.
Remove the VPC from the hub and re-add it as a hybrid spoke.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC spokes support export filters (exclude or include ranges) that control which subnet routes are shared with the hub.
questions.distractor_summary: Firewall rules block traffic but still leak routes, dynamic routing mode doesn't apply to individual subnets, and hybrid spokes are for VPN, Interconnect, or router appliances.
