questions.question: A central networking team owns an NCC hub in the `net-hub` project. An application team adds its VPC, in a different project, as a VPC spoke. The spoke is created but remains inactive, and no routes are exchanged. What is required?
options: A hub administrator must review and accept the spoke proposal from the other project.
The application team must enable global dynamic routing on its own VPC in every region.
The spoke must be recreated in the `net-hub` project before it can join in every region.
A Cloud Router must be created in the application VPC for the spoke for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: VPC spokes from a different project than the hub are created as proposals that the hub administrator must accept before they become active.
questions.distractor_summary: Dynamic routing mode and Cloud Routers aren't required for VPC spokes, and cross-project spokes are supported without moving resources.

questions.question: A company connects offices in London and Singapore to Google Cloud with HA VPN tunnels in `europe-west2` and `asia-southeast1`. Both tunnel pairs are added as hybrid spokes to an NCC hub, but traffic between the two offices doesn't use Google's backbone—the offices still can't reach each other through Google Cloud. What is missing?
options: Use VPC Network Peering between the two regions to carry the traffic between sites overall.
Use a router appliance spoke in each region to carry the traffic between sites overall.
Enable site-to-site data transfer on both hybrid spokes, in regions that support it.
Use global dynamic routing mode on the hub to carry the traffic between sites.
questions.correct_rationale: For hybrid spokes to exchange routes and exchange traffic with each other across Google's network, site-to-site data transfer must be enabled on the spokes, and it's available only in supported regions.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering doesn't apply to on-premises sites, router appliances aren't required when using Cloud VPN, and the hub itself has no dynamic routing mode.

questions.question: An engineer deploys a third-party SD-WAN virtual appliance in a VPC and registers it as an NCC router appliance spoke. BGP sessions come up, but traffic from branches destined for VMs in the VPC is dropped at the appliance, even though the appliance forwards packets correctly in its own logs. What configuration is most likely missing?
options: Use a Cloud NAT gateway for the appliance subnet so the appliance can forward traffic.
Use Private Google Access on the appliance subnet so the appliance can forward traffic.
Use a proxy-only subnet in the region for the appliance to forward traffic.
Enable IP forwarding (`canIpForward`) on the router appliance VM so it can forward traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: Router appliance VMs send and receive packets whose source or destination isn't their own IP, which Google Cloud drops unless IP forwarding is enabled on the instance.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud NAT, Private Google Access, and proxy-only subnets don't affect forwarding of transit traffic.

questions.question: A company has 30 non-overlapping VPCs and a data center connected over Dedicated Interconnect in a `transit-vpc`. It has hit VPC Network Peering limits and wants every VPC and the data center to be able to reach each other through one managed construct. What should the engineer design?
options: Replace the Interconnect with HA VPN in each of the VPCs for the connectivity for the team.
Use an NCC hub with the 30 VPCs as VPC spokes and the VLAN attachments as hybrid spokes.
Use Shared VPC with all 30 of the VPCs merged into the transit VPC.
Use Cloud Router route advertisements from each of the VPCs over VPC peering for the team.
questions.correct_rationale: NCC supports route exchange between VPC spokes and hybrid spokes, providing a scalable transit for both VPC-to-VPC and VPC-to-on-premises traffic without peering limits.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-VPC VPN is costly and duplicative, merging VPCs is a large redesign, and Cloud Routers don't advertise routes over peering.

questions.question: Adding a newly acquired VPC as an NCC VPC spoke fails because its `172.16.8.0/24` subnet overlaps with a subnet in an existing spoke. That subnet in the new VPC hosts only a legacy tool that doesn't need to be reachable from other spokes. What is the fastest way to attach the VPC?
options: Use an export exclusion filter for `172.16.8.0/24` on the new spoke.
Use VPC Network Peering instead of NCC for the newly acquired VPC.
Expand the existing spoke's subnet so that it absorbs the overlapping range.
Enable Private Google Access on the overlapping subnet of the new VPC.
questions.correct_rationale: Excluding the overlapping range from the spoke's exported routes removes the conflict so the rest of the VPC can attach.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering also rejects overlapping subnets, expanding a subnet can't resolve overlap, and Private Google Access doesn't affect route exchange.

questions.question: A GKE application behind an external Application Load Balancer created by an Ingress shows uneven load and extra latency. Traffic reaches nodes on a NodePort and is then forwarded by kube-proxy to Pods on other nodes. The team wants the load balancer to send traffic directly to Pods and health-check them individually. What should the engineer implement?
options: Change the Service type to `LoadBalancer` with `externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster` for the app.
Deploy an Nginx ingress controller as a DaemonSet on all of the cluster nodes.
Use container-native load balancing with NEGs (`cloud.google.com/neg`) on a VPC-native cluster.
Increase the number of nodes in the cluster so that the load is spread out.
questions.correct_rationale: Container-native load balancing uses zonal NEGs of Pod IPs so the load balancer targets and health-checks Pods directly, removing the extra node hop.
questions.distractor_summary: A `LoadBalancer` Service with `Cluster` policy still uses node-level forwarding, a self-managed ingress adds a proxy layer, and more nodes don't remove the double hop.

questions.question: A platform team wants one global external load balancer shared by several application teams on a GKE cluster. The platform team must control the load balancer, certificates, and listeners, while each app team manages routing for its own hostnames in its own namespace. What should the engineer use?
options: Use one Ingress resource per namespace, each creating its own load balancer.
Use the GKE Gateway controller with a platform-owned `Gateway` and team-owned `HTTPRoute` resources.
Use a single Ingress resource in the platform namespace that the app teams edit across the subscriptions.
Use a `LoadBalancer` Service per team with Cloud DNS weighted records for the teams for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: The Gateway API separates roles: platform operators own the `Gateway` and its listeners, and app teams attach `HTTPRoute` resources from their own namespaces to a shared load balancer.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-namespace Ingresses create separate load balancers, a single shared Ingress breaks role separation, and `LoadBalancer` Services are L4 and don't share one L7 entry point.

questions.question: A security team requires an audit trail of Kubernetes NetworkPolicy decisions, including which connections were allowed or denied between Pods, sent to Cloud Logging. The cluster is being created now. What should the engineer do?
options: Enable VPC Flow Logs on the node subnet of the cluster to see the decisions.
Enable Firewall Rules Logging on the firewall rules that GKE manages for the cluster.
Deploy Calico with its flow-log add-on on the cluster to log the decisions.
Create the cluster with GKE Dataplane V2 and enable network policy logging on it.
questions.correct_rationale: GKE Dataplane V2 supports network policy logging, which records allowed and denied connections evaluated by NetworkPolicy and exports them to Cloud Logging.
questions.distractor_summary: VPC Flow Logs and firewall logging don't show NetworkPolicy decisions, and Calico can't be combined with Dataplane V2's built-in enforcement.

questions.question: In a GKE cluster with NetworkPolicy enforcement enabled, the `backend` namespace has a default-deny ingress policy. Pods labeled `app=api` in `backend` must accept TCP 8080 only from any Pod in the namespace labeled `team=frontend`. What NetworkPolicy should the engineer create in the `backend` namespace?
options: Use `podSelector: app=api` with ingress `from: namespaceSelector: team=frontend` on TCP 8080.
Use `podSelector: {}` with ingress `from: podSelector: team=frontend` on TCP 8080.
Use `podSelector: app=api` with egress to `namespaceSelector: team=frontend` on TCP 8080 overall.
Use a VPC firewall rule that allows TCP 8080 from the Pod range to the node range.
questions.correct_rationale: Selecting the `api` Pods and allowing ingress from a `namespaceSelector` matching the frontend namespace's label admits only those sources on port 8080.
questions.distractor_summary: A bare `podSelector` in `from` matches Pods in the same namespace and the empty selector opens all backend Pods, an egress rule controls the wrong direction, and VPC firewall rules don't enforce Pod-level namespace policy.

questions.question: A compliance team uses VPC Flow Logs to monitor GKE traffic. They notice that communication between Pods running on the same node never appears in the logs. What should the engineer enable?
options: Increase the VPC Flow Logs sampling rate to 1.0 for the node subnet.
Enable Packet Mirroring on the node subnet so that the traffic is copied for the application.
Enable intranode visibility on the cluster so that Pod-to-Pod traffic appears in the logs.
Enable metadata annotations on VPC Flow Logs to add the Pod information for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Pod-to-Pod traffic on the same node doesn't leave the node, so VPC networking never sees it unless intranode visibility routes it through the VPC fabric.
questions.distractor_summary: Raising sampling or adding metadata can't log traffic that isn't observed, and Packet Mirroring has the same visibility gap.

questions.question: A GKE cluster in `us-central1` exposes an internal Service using a `LoadBalancer` Service with the `networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal"` annotation. Clients in `us-central1` connect successfully, but VMs in `us-east1` in the same VPC time out. What should the engineer do?
options: Change the Service to `type: NodePort` and use the node addresses instead for the application.
Create a firewall rule that allows traffic from the `us-east1` subnets to the nodes overall.
Enable global dynamic routing mode on the VPC that hosts the cluster across the subscriptions.
Add the `internal-load-balancer-allow-global-access` annotation to the Service to enable global access.
questions.correct_rationale: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers only accept clients from the same region unless global access is enabled, which the annotation does for GKE Services.
questions.distractor_summary: NodePort doesn't solve regional access, firewall rules can't override the regional restriction, and dynamic routing mode affects Cloud Router routes.

questions.question: A retailer runs identical GKE clusters in `us-east1` and `europe-west1`, both registered to a fleet. It wants one global anycast IP that routes users to the closest healthy cluster and automatically fails over if a cluster's Pods become unavailable. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use two regional external Application Load Balancers with Cloud DNS geolocation routing.
Use a Multi-cluster Gateway or Multi Cluster Ingress with a config cluster and a global ALB.
Use an external passthrough Network Load Balancer in each of the regions.
Use Cloud Service Mesh with a single-cluster Ingress in the primary region.
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-cluster Gateway and Multi Cluster Ingress program a global external Application Load Balancer across fleet clusters, giving one anycast IP with proximity routing and health-based failover.
questions.distractor_summary: DNS-based routing depends on TTLs and exposes multiple IPs, regional passthrough load balancers aren't global, and a single-cluster Ingress doesn't span clusters.

questions.question: A fintech company's security team requires mutual TLS between all microservices across two GKE clusters, fine-grained authorization based on service identity, and traffic telemetry, without changing application code. What should the engineer implement?
options: Use Cloud Service Mesh with sidecar injection or a managed data plane and mTLS enforcement policies.
Use Kubernetes NetworkPolicy with default-deny rules between all of the services.
Use Cloud NGFW Enterprise with TLS inspection between the Pods of the services by default.
Use internal Application Load Balancers in front of every one of the services for the team.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Service Mesh provides transparent mTLS, identity-based authorization policies, and telemetry for services without code changes, across clusters.
questions.distractor_summary: NetworkPolicy works at L3/L4 without encryption or service identity, NGFW inspects rather than provides service mTLS, and fronting each service with a load balancer doesn't give mutual authentication.

questions.question: A private GKE cluster's nodes can reach the internet through Cloud NAT, but Pods can't reach external package repositories. The Cloud NAT gateway was configured by selecting the node subnet's primary IP range only. What should the engineer change?
options: Assign external IP addresses to the nodes so that the Pods can reach the internet.
Enable Private Google Access on the node subnet so that the Pods can reach the internet overall.
Update Cloud NAT to include the subnet's secondary Pod ranges, or all IP ranges of the subnet.
Configure ip-masq-agent to masquerade all traffic to node IPs and remove Cloud NAT.
questions.correct_rationale: Pods in VPC-native clusters send egress traffic from Pod IPs in secondary ranges, so Cloud NAT must be configured for those ranges in addition to the primary range.
questions.distractor_summary: External IPs on nodes violate the private design, Private Google Access only covers Google APIs, and removing Cloud NAT would leave private nodes with no internet egress.

questions.question: An auditor asks for logs of all denied inbound connection attempts to VMs in a VPC. Firewall Rules Logging is enabled on every custom rule, but denied connections that don't match any custom rule aren't logged. What should the engineer do?
options: Enable logging on the implied deny ingress rule for the VPC network for the application.
Create an explicit deny-all ingress rule at priority 65534 and enable logging on it.
Enable VPC Flow Logs with a sampling rate of 1.0 on every subnet of the VPC as needed.
Enable Packet Mirroring for all of the VMs and inspect the mirrored traffic as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Implied rules can't have logging enabled, so an explicit, logged deny-all rule at a low priority captures traffic that would otherwise hit the implied deny.
questions.distractor_summary: VPC Flow Logs record accepted flows rather than firewall deny decisions, and Packet Mirroring is costly and doesn't record firewall actions.

questions.question: A PCI workload's VMs must not send traffic to the internet, but they must reach internal services in `10.0.0.0/8` and Google APIs via `private.googleapis.com`. The engineer wants a firewall-based control. Which set of egress rules meets the requirement?
options: Allow egress to `10.0.0.0/8` at 65000; deny egress `0.0.0.0/0` at 1000 for the workload overall.
Deny egress `0.0.0.0/0` at 1000; allow egress to `10.0.0.0/8` and `199.36.153.8/30` at 65000 overall.
Rely on the implied egress deny rule and add allow rules for `10.0.0.0/8` only.
questions.correct_rationale: Lower priority numbers are evaluated first, so the specific allow rules at priority 1000 permit internal and API traffic before the broad deny at 65000 blocks everything else.
questions.distractor_summary: Options B and C place the deny ahead of the allows, blocking required traffic, and the implied egress rule is allow, not deny.

questions.question: A VPC has an ingress rule allowing TCP 443 from `0.0.0.0/0` to web servers and an egress rule denying all traffic from those servers. Clients initiate HTTPS connections to the web servers. What happens?
options: Connections fail because the egress deny rule blocks the return traffic.
Connections succeed only if an egress allow rule for the ephemeral ports is added across the subscriptions.
Connections succeed because firewall rules are stateful and allow return traffic for allowed connections.
Connections succeed only for the IPv6 clients that reach the web servers.
questions.correct_rationale: Google Cloud firewall rules are stateful, so once an ingress connection is allowed, response traffic is permitted regardless of egress rules.
questions.distractor_summary: Ephemeral-port egress rules are needed with stateless ACLs, not with VPC firewalls, and IP version doesn't change stateful behavior.

questions.question: A company wants to move 400 VPC firewall rules into a global network firewall policy to use secure tags and FQDN objects, with minimal risk of accidental exposure. What's the recommended approach?
options: Delete the VPC firewall rules and recreate each of them manually in the new policy.
Use the `gcloud` firewall migration tooling to generate, review and associate the policy, then retire legacy rules.
Create a hierarchical firewall policy with the same rules at the organization level.
Disable all of the VPC firewall rules and rely on Cloud Armor for filtering.
questions.correct_rationale: Google provides a migration tool that converts VPC firewall rules into a network firewall policy, letting teams review and validate before cutting over via the enforcement order and removing legacy rules.
questions.distractor_summary: Manual recreation is error-prone, moving VPC-specific rules to the organization level changes their scope, and Cloud Armor protects load balancers rather than VM-level east-west traffic.

questions.question: A security team maintains a list of 60 partner IP ranges that must be allowed in rules across multiple firewall policies. The list changes monthly, and updates currently require editing many rules. What should the engineer use?
options: Use network tags on every partner-facing VM in the projects overall.
Use a Cloud Armor security policy that lists the partner ranges.
Use a single firewall rule per partner range in each of the policies.
Use an address group that the firewall policy rules reference.
questions.correct_rationale: Address groups are reusable collections of IP ranges that can be referenced in firewall policy rules, so one update propagates to every rule that uses the group.
questions.distractor_summary: Network tags identify targets rather than external sources, Cloud Armor only applies at load balancers, and one rule per range increases management overhead.

questions.question: A company has VMs with external IP addresses that aren't behind a load balancer. The security team wants to block inbound connections from specific countries and from known malicious IP addresses maintained by Google, without maintaining IP lists themselves. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use network firewall policy rules with geolocation objects and Google Threat Intelligence lists as sources.
Attach Cloud Armor security policies directly to the VMs that have the external IPs for the application.
Use VPC firewall rules with manually maintained lists of country IP ranges throughout the organization.
Use Cloud NAT rules that drop the traffic by its source country of origin.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud NGFW firewall policies support geolocation objects and Google-managed Threat Intelligence lists, which are updated automatically.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Armor attaches to load balancer backends rather than standalone VMs, manually maintained lists are error-prone, and Cloud NAT handles outbound translation rather than inbound filtering.

questions.question: A company deployed Cloud NGFW Enterprise with an intrusion prevention security profile. Test attacks sent over plain HTTP are detected and blocked, but the same attacks sent over HTTPS pass through undetected. What should the engineer do?
options: Increase the threat severity level in the security profile to "critical" for the endpoint in every region.
Enable Firewall Rules Logging on the rules that apply the security profile group.
Configure TLS inspection with a CAS CA pool and policy, enable it on rules, and distribute the CA cert.
Replace the firewall endpoint with Cloud Armor in front of the workloads.
questions.correct_rationale: Encrypted payloads can't be inspected until Cloud NGFW Enterprise decrypts them with TLS inspection, which uses Certificate Authority Service and requires clients to trust the issuing CA. Severity settings and logging don't provide decryption, and Cloud Armor protects load balancers rather than inspecting VM traffic.

questions.question: A company enabled Cloud NGFW Enterprise intrusion prevention for a VPC. VMs in `us-central1-a` are protected, but VMs in `us-central1-b` and `us-central1-c` aren't being inspected, even though the firewall policy rule with `apply_security_profile_group` targets all VMs. What's the cause?
options: Security profiles only apply to the first zone in a region where they are used for the application.
The firewall policy must be regional rather than global for the endpoint across the subscriptions.
The rule's priority is lower than the implied allow egress rule for the VMs across the subscriptions.
Firewall endpoints are zonal, so each zone with workloads needs an endpoint and VPC association.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud NGFW Enterprise firewall endpoints are zonal resources, and traffic is only inspected in zones where an endpoint exists and is associated with the VPC. Security profiles apply in all zones with endpoints, both global and regional policies can reference profiles, and implied rules have the lowest priority.

questions.question: A regional internal Application Load Balancer fronts VMs. Health checks pass, but client requests forwarded by the load balancer are rejected at the backends. Firewall rules allow health check ranges and client subnets. What additional ingress rule is required?
options: Allow ingress from `35.235.240.0/20` to the backends on the serving ports for the team.
Allow ingress from the proxy-only subnet range to the backends on the serving ports used.
Allow ingress from `0.0.0.0/0` to the backends on the serving ports.
Allow ingress from the load balancer's forwarding rule IP to the backends for the team.
questions.correct_rationale: Envoy proxies for internal Application Load Balancers connect to backends from the proxy-only subnet, so backends must allow ingress from that range.
questions.distractor_summary: The IAP range is for TCP forwarding, opening to the internet violates least privilege, and the forwarding rule IP isn't the source of proxied connections.

questions.question: A media company is consolidating two websites behind one global external Application Load Balancer. Requests to `www.example.com/api/*` must go to a GKE service exposed through zonal NEGs, requests to `www.example.com/static/*` must be served from a Cloud Storage bucket, and all requests to `shop.example.com` must go to a Compute Engine managed instance group. How should the engineer configure the load balancer?
options: Create three forwarding rules with different IP addresses, one for each backend.
Create a URL map: `www` routes `/api/*` to NEGs and `/static/*` to a bucket; `shop` to the MIG.
Create one backend service with the NEGs, bucket and MIG, separating traffic with balancing modes.
Use Cloud DNS routing policies to send each path to a different load balancer.
questions.correct_rationale: URL maps use host rules and path matchers to route by hostname and path to different backend services and backend buckets behind a single IP. Separate forwarding rules aren't necessary, a backend service can't contain a Cloud Storage bucket or mix these backend types for path routing, and DNS can't route by URL path.

questions.question: A global external Application Load Balancer has a backend service with managed instance groups in `us-east1` and `us-west1`. The team must perform maintenance on the `us-east1` MIG and wants new requests to shift to `us-west1` without deleting the backend or changing the MIG size. What should the engineer do?
options: Delete the health check so that the backend is marked as unhealthy for the traffic.
Change the balancing mode of the `us-east1` backend to `CONNECTION` for the service.
Remove the `us-east1` firewall rule for the health check ranges for the backend.
Set the capacity scaler of the `us-east1` backend to 0 to drain its traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: Setting a backend's capacity scaler to 0 stops the load balancer from sending it new requests while keeping the backend configured, which is the intended way to drain it.
questions.distractor_summary: Deleting the health check or blocking health check traffic forces failures instead of a controlled drain, and changing the balancing mode doesn't remove capacity.

questions.question: A B2B web application behind a global external Application Load Balancer uses client IP session affinity to keep users on the same backend. Customers report that almost all traffic from a large enterprise customer lands on a single overloaded VM. That customer's users reach the internet through a few corporate NAT addresses. What should the engineer change?
options: Switch session affinity to generated cookie affinity for the web application backend.
Switch session affinity to none and store the sessions on the local disk overall.
Increase the maximum requests per second for the overloaded VM in the backend.
Change the balancing mode to `UTILIZATION` on the backend of the service.
questions.correct_rationale: Client IP affinity maps all users behind the same NAT address to the same backend, while generated cookie affinity keys on a per-client cookie set by the load balancer and spreads users evenly.
questions.distractor_summary: Removing affinity breaks sessions stored locally, and changing capacity or balancing mode doesn't change affinity-based concentration.

questions.question: A company deploys the same Cloud Run service in `us-central1`, `europe-west1`, and `asia-east1`. It wants a single global IP, a custom domain with a managed certificate, Cloud Armor protection, and routing to the nearest region. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a regional external Application Load Balancer in each region with an internet NEG to Cloud Run.
Use a Cloud Run domain mapping in each region with Cloud DNS geolocation routing overall.
Use a global external Application Load Balancer with one serverless NEG per region.
Use an external passthrough Network Load Balancer with Cloud Run as the backend overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Serverless NEGs are regional, so a global external Application Load Balancer backend service with one serverless NEG per region provides a single anycast IP, proximity routing, managed certificates, and Cloud Armor.
questions.distractor_summary: Regional load balancers or domain mappings don't give a single global entry point with Cloud Armor, and passthrough Network Load Balancers don't support serverless backends.

questions.question: A retailer is migrating a web application from its data center to Compute Engine over six months. The data center connects via Dedicated Interconnect. The company wants one global external Application Load Balancer that sends 90% of traffic to on-premises servers and 10% to Google Cloud initially, adjusting weights over time. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use an internet NEG for the on-premises public IPs together with a MIG backend across the subscriptions.
Use two separate load balancers with weighted Cloud DNS records between them across the subscriptions.
Use Private Service Connect to publish the on-premises servers to the load balancer for the application.
Use a hybrid connectivity NEG with on-premises endpoints and a MIG, split by weights in the URL map.
questions.correct_rationale: Hybrid connectivity NEGs let load balancers send traffic to on-premises endpoints over Interconnect or VPN, and URL map weighted backend services control the migration split.
questions.distractor_summary: Internet NEGs send traffic over the public internet, DNS weighting is less precise and TTL-dependent, and PSC is for publishing services to consumers rather than load balancing on-premises backends.

questions.question: A company hosts product images on a third-party object storage provider with a public HTTPS endpoint. It wants those images served through its existing global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN, under the same domain as its main site. What backend should the engineer use for the image path?
options: Use a backend bucket that points to the third-party provider's storage.
Use a backend service with a global internet NEG holding the provider's FQDN and port 443.
Use a hybrid connectivity NEG that holds the provider's public IP addresses in every region.
Use a serverless NEG that proxies the requests to the provider's storage for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Internet NEGs define external endpoints (FQDN or IP and port) as backends, allowing Cloud CDN to cache content from origins outside Google Cloud.
questions.distractor_summary: Backend buckets only reference Cloud Storage, hybrid NEGs are for private endpoints reached over hybrid connectivity, and serverless NEGs point to Cloud Run, App Engine, or Cloud Functions.

questions.question: A payments team wants to release version 2 of its checkout API gradually. Both versions run as separate backend services behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Initially, 5% of requests should go to v2 and 95% to v1, with the split changed through configuration only. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a URL map route rule with weighted backend services, 95 to v1 and 5 to v2.
Use two backends in one backend service with capacity scalers of 0.95 and 0.05.
Use two forwarding rules and let the clients select which version they call.
Use a Cloud Armor rule that redirects 5% of the requests to version 2.
questions.correct_rationale: URL map route actions support weighted backend services for traffic splitting, which is the standard canary mechanism for Application Load Balancers.
questions.distractor_summary: Capacity scalers adjust capacity rather than enforce precise percentages across services, multiple forwarding rules push the decision to clients, and Cloud Armor doesn't perform percentage-based routing.

questions.question: A company is rewriting its recommendation service and wants to test the new version with real production traffic without affecting users. Responses from the new version must be discarded. Both versions sit behind the same global external Application Load Balancer. What feature should the engineer use?
options: Use weighted traffic splitting at 1% to the new version of the service.
Use Packet Mirroring from the production backends to the new version of the service.
Use request mirroring in the URL map route action, targeting the new backend service.
Use header-based routing that sends requests with a test header to the new version.
questions.correct_rationale: Request mirroring copies requests to a shadow backend service and discards its responses, so users are unaffected while the new version receives real traffic.
questions.distractor_summary: Traffic splitting sends real users to the new version, Packet Mirroring copies packets to a collector rather than to an application, and header-based routing only covers requests that include the header.

questions.question: A company is migrating `*.shop.example.com` from another provider to a global external Application Load Balancer. It wants a Google-managed wildcard certificate that is active before DNS is switched, to avoid any TLS errors during cutover. What should the engineer do?
options: Create a classic Google-managed SSL certificate on the target proxy, then switch DNS.
Upload a self-managed certificate generated with OpenSSL for the wildcard.
Enable Cloud CDN, which provisions the certificates automatically for the domain.
Use Certificate Manager with DNS authorization for a managed wildcard cert, then switch DNS.
questions.correct_rationale: Certificate Manager DNS authorization validates domain control through a CNAME record, supporting wildcard certificates and issuance before traffic points to the load balancer.
questions.distractor_summary: Classic load-balancer-authorized managed certificates require DNS to point to the load balancer and don't support wildcards, a self-signed certificate triggers browser errors, and Cloud CDN doesn't issue certificates.

questions.question: A company runs a single-VM virtual router appliance that must receive traffic on three separate external IP addresses, each for a different customer, on the same protocols and ports. Load balancing isn't needed. What is the simplest way to deliver traffic for all three IPs to the VM?
options: Attach three network interfaces to the VM, each with its own external IP address in production.
Create three forwarding rules with protocol forwarding to a target instance that uses the VM.
Create an external passthrough Network Load Balancer with three backend services.
Assign alias IP ranges that have public addresses to the primary interface of the VM as needed.
questions.correct_rationale: Protocol forwarding uses forwarding rules with target instances to send traffic for multiple external IPs to a single VM without load balancing.
questions.distractor_summary: Extra NICs must be in different VPCs, a load balancer adds unneeded complexity, and alias IP ranges are internal.

questions.question: A retailer wants to enable Cloud Armor's preconfigured SQL injection rules on its checkout backend right before a major sale, but it's worried about false positives blocking real customers. What's the recommended approach?
options: Deploy `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf('sqli-v33-stable')` in preview mode, tune from the logs, then enforce it.
Deploy the rule at the highest sensitivity level with a deny action to block all attacks.
Deploy the rule only on the default rule of the security policy for the checkout.
Enable Adaptive Protection instead, since it does not produce false positives for traffic for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: Preview mode logs what a rule would do without enforcing it, letting teams tune sensitivity levels and opt out of noisy signatures before blocking.
questions.distractor_summary: Starting at maximum sensitivity maximizes false positives, the default rule is a catch-all allow or deny, and Adaptive Protection detects volumetric L7 attacks rather than replacing WAF signatures.

questions.question: A company serves downloads from a Cloud Storage backend bucket through Cloud CDN. It needs to block requests from sanctioned countries, including requests that would be served from the CDN cache. A backend security policy with a geo-deny rule was attached, but cached content is still served to blocked countries. What should the engineer do?
options: Disable Cloud CDN for the bucket so that the policy applies to the origin traffic as needed.
Add the geo-deny rule to the backend security policy with a higher priority number in Azure.
Create an edge security policy with the geo-deny rule and attach it to the backend bucket.
Set the bucket to uniform bucket-level access and deny the countries in the bucket policy overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Edge security policies are evaluated before the CDN cache and can be attached to backend buckets, so they filter both cached and uncached requests.
questions.distractor_summary: Backend security policies apply only to requests sent to the origin, disabling CDN sacrifices performance, and bucket IAM settings don't filter by geography.

questions.question: A news site suffers intermittent application-layer DDoS attacks that use valid-looking HTTP GET requests from thousands of IPs. The security team can't write static rules fast enough. They want Cloud Armor to detect anomalous traffic, generate a signature, and optionally deploy a mitigating rule automatically. What should the engineer enable?
options: Use rate limiting with a `rate_based_ban` rule that is keyed on the IP address in every region.
Use Adaptive Protection on the backend security policy, with auto-deploy of suggested rules.
Use advanced network DDoS protection on the backend service of the load balancer for the team.
Use preconfigured WAF rules for protocol attacks on the load balancer policy.
questions.correct_rationale: Adaptive Protection uses machine learning to detect L7 anomalies, generates attack signatures and suggested rules, and can auto-deploy them.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-IP rate limiting is weak against thousands of distributed sources, advanced network DDoS protection targets L3/L4 attacks, and WAF signatures don't detect well-formed volumetric floods.

questions.question: A SaaS company exposes an API behind a global external Application Load Balancer. Each customer sends requests with its own `X-API-Key` header, and many customers share NAT IPs. Each customer must be limited to 500 requests per minute, with excess requests receiving HTTP 429 while traffic under the limit continues. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a `rate_based_ban` rule keyed on the client IP with a ban duration of 10 minutes.
Use an Adaptive Protection policy with a threshold of 500 requests per minute for each key.
Use a deny rule that matches the requests that arrive without the API key header.
Use a `throttle` rule keyed on the `X-API-Key` header at 500 per 60 seconds with `deny(429)`.
questions.correct_rationale: A throttle rule keyed on an HTTP header limits each API key separately and returns 429 only for requests above the threshold.
questions.distractor_summary: Keying on client IP would penalize customers sharing NAT addresses, a ban blocks all traffic for the duration, and Adaptive Protection doesn't enforce per-customer quotas.

questions.question: A game company runs UDP game servers on VMs with external IPs and behind external passthrough Network Load Balancers. It's experiencing volumetric L3/L4 DDoS attacks and wants Cloud Armor to filter traffic at Google's edge before it reaches the VMs, including custom packet-level filters. What should the engineer configure?
options: Enroll in Cloud Armor Enterprise, enable advanced network DDoS protection and add a network edge policy.
Attach a backend security policy with preconfigured WAF rules to the passthrough load balancer by default.
Put the game servers behind a global external Application Load Balancer instead of passthrough.
Create VPC firewall rules that deny UDP from the unknown sources to the game servers.
questions.correct_rationale: Advanced network DDoS protection and network edge security policies, available with Cloud Armor Enterprise, filter traffic for passthrough Network Load Balancers, protocol forwarding, and VMs with public IPs at the edge.
questions.distractor_summary: Backend security policies and WAF rules apply to proxy-based load balancers, Application Load Balancers don't support UDP game traffic, and VPC firewall rules act at the VM rather than at the edge.

questions.question: An online ticketing company is targeted by scalper bots during ticket releases. It wants suspicious clients challenged with a CAPTCHA-style assessment while legitimate users are unaffected, using its global external Application Load Balancer. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a deny rule for all of the traffic from the cloud provider IP ranges.
Use a throttle rule of 10 requests per minute for each of the client IP addresses in production.
Use Cloud Armor bot management with reCAPTCHA Enterprise, redirect challenges and token rules.
Use Identity-Aware Proxy in front of the ticketing site for all of the visitors in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Armor integrates with reCAPTCHA Enterprise to redirect suspicious traffic to challenges and to evaluate token scores in rules, targeting bots without blocking real users.
questions.distractor_summary: Blocking cloud ranges misses residential bots, aggressive throttling hurts legitimate users, and IAP requires authentication, which isn't appropriate for public ticket buyers.

questions.question: A Cloud Armor policy has a rule at priority 500 that denies traffic from country code `XX`, and a rule at priority 1000 that allows a partner's IP range `198.51.100.0/24`. The partner's range is located in country `XX`, and its requests are being blocked. What should the engineer do?
options: Change the default rule to allow so that the partner traffic is no longer denied overall.
Change the partner allow rule's priority to a number lower than 500, such as 100.
Change the geo-deny rule to `deny(403)` in place of `deny(404)` for the country overall.
Move the partner allow rule into a separate policy attached to the same backend overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud Armor evaluates rules in priority order and stops at the first match, so the partner allow rule must have a lower priority number than the geo-deny rule.
questions.distractor_summary: The default rule only applies when no other rule matches, the deny status code doesn't affect matching, and a backend service can have only one backend security policy.

questions.question: An e-commerce site uses Cloud CDN, but its cache hit ratio is low. Analysis shows that the same product image is requested with different marketing query parameters such as `utm_source` and `utm_campaign`, creating separate cache entries. Only the `size` parameter changes the image. What should the engineer configure?
options: Set the cache mode to `FORCE_CACHE_ALL` on the backend service of the site.
Enable negative caching on the backend service so that more requests are cached.
Exclude the host from the cache key so that more requests are served from the cache.
Configure the cache key to include only the `size` query parameter for the images.
questions.correct_rationale: Customizing the cache key to include only relevant query parameters ensures that requests differing only by tracking parameters share a cache entry.
questions.distractor_summary: Forcing caching of all content doesn't fix key fragmentation, negative caching applies to error responses, and removing the host doesn't address query-string variation.

questions.question: A company deploys front-end updates to a Cloud CDN-fronted site several times per hour and invalidates `/assets/*` after each deployment. Invalidations sometimes take minutes, and the team occasionally hits invalidation rate limits, causing users to see stale JavaScript. What's the recommended approach?
options: Set the default TTL for the assets to 0 so they are always fetched fresh.
Invalidate the entire cache (`/*`) after each of the deployments of the site by default.
Use versioned or content-hashed asset filenames, and keep invalidation for exceptions.
Disable Cloud CDN during each deployment of the front end and re-enable it after overall.
questions.correct_rationale: Google recommends versioned URLs for frequently changing content because they bypass stale cache entries immediately, while invalidation is rate-limited and not instant.
questions.distractor_summary: A TTL of 0 eliminates caching benefits, full invalidations are slower and still rate-limited, and disabling CDN during deployments disrupts performance.

questions.question: After a product catalog was reorganized, bots began requesting thousands of old URLs that now return HTTP 404 from the origin. The requests bypass Cloud CDN's cache and overload the origin servers. The URLs will never exist again. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a Cloud Armor rule that blocks all of the 404 responses from the origin.
Use negative caching with a TTL for the 404 responses of the origin.
Use larger instance types for the origin so that it can absorb the bot traffic.
Use a cache key that excludes the request path so that more requests match.
questions.correct_rationale: Negative caching lets Cloud CDN cache error responses such as 404 for a set TTL, so repeated requests for missing URLs are served from cache instead of reaching the origin.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Armor matches requests rather than origin responses, scaling the origin treats a symptom, and removing the path from the cache key would serve wrong content.

questions.question: A company stores media in a private Amazon S3 bucket and wants to serve it through Cloud CDN via an internet NEG without making the bucket public. How should the engineer allow Cloud CDN to fetch from the private bucket?
options: Make the bucket public and restrict access to it with a Cloud Armor policy for the application.
Use Cloud CDN signed URLs, which S3 accepts natively for the bucket content for the application.
Copy all of the content to Cloud Storage with Storage Transfer Service first for the application.
Configure private origin authentication with AWS Signature V4 and an HMAC key for the bucket.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud CDN supports private origin authentication for Amazon S3-compatible origins using AWS Signature Version 4, letting it fetch objects from private buckets.
questions.distractor_summary: Making the bucket public violates the requirement, Cloud CDN signed URLs control client access and aren't understood by S3, and migrating the data is unnecessary.

questions.question: A training company sells video courses stored in a Cloud Storage bucket behind a backend bucket with Cloud CDN. It plans to use Cloud CDN signed URLs so only paying users can access content, and it wants to prevent users from bypassing the CDN and accessing the bucket directly. What should the engineer do?
options: Create a signed URL key on the backend bucket, make it private, and grant the CDN fill account object viewer.
Keep the bucket public and use signed URLs only for the premium videos.
Use Cloud Storage signed URLs in place of the Cloud CDN signed URLs for the videos throughout the organization.
Attach an edge security policy that denies requests without a valid session cookie throughout the organization.
questions.correct_rationale: With a signing key on the backend bucket and a private bucket readable only by the Cloud CDN fill service account, content is accessible only through valid Cloud CDN signed URLs.
questions.distractor_summary: A public bucket allows direct access, Cloud Storage signed URLs bypass the CDN, and Cloud Armor can't validate application session cookies.

questions.question: A company enables DNSSEC on its Cloud DNS public zone `example.com`. Afterward, validating resolvers return SERVFAIL for the domain, even though the zone's records are correct. What is the most likely cause?
options: Cloud DNS does not support DNSSEC with TXT records in the zone.
The DS record at the registrar is missing or does not match the zone's key-signing key.
The SOA record TTL of the zone is too low for resolvers to validate the zone for the team.
DNSSEC requires a private zone that has the same name as the public zone.
questions.correct_rationale: After enabling DNSSEC, the DS record for the zone's key-signing key must be published at the registrar to establish the chain of trust; a mismatched DS record makes validating resolvers fail.
questions.distractor_summary: TXT records are supported, the SOA TTL doesn't break validation, and DNSSEC applies to public zones.

questions.question: A company is migrating 40 zones from on-premises BIND servers to Cloud DNS public zones with minimal disruption. What is the recommended migration sequence?
options: Update the NS records at the registrar first, then create the Cloud DNS zones and records.
Recreate every record by hand in the console, then delete the BIND servers.
Export the BIND zone files, import them with `gcloud`, verify, lower the NS TTLs, then update the registrar.
Create forwarding zones in Cloud DNS that point permanently to the BIND servers.
questions.correct_rationale: Importing BIND zone files, verifying resolution against Cloud DNS's name servers, and lowering TTLs before changing delegation at the registrar minimizes outage risk.
questions.distractor_summary: Changing NS records first would send queries to empty zones, manual recreation is error-prone, and forwarding zones are for private resolution rather than hosting public zones.

questions.question: To route all VM DNS queries through a corporate DNS security appliance, an engineer created a DNS server policy with alternative name servers set to the appliance's IP. Afterward, VMs can resolve public names, but Cloud DNS private zones and Compute Engine internal DNS names (`*.internal`) no longer resolve. Why?
options: Alternative name servers replace Cloud DNS resolution, so private and forwarding zones are bypassed.
Private zones must be re-authorized after a server policy is created on the VPC across the subscriptions.
The appliance needs a firewall rule that allows `35.199.192.0/19` into the VPC across the subscriptions.
Internal DNS names only resolve when Private Google Access is enabled for the subnet for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: When a server policy specifies alternative name servers, VMs' queries go to those servers instead of Cloud DNS's normal resolution order, so private zones and internal DNS stop working unless the alternative servers forward back through an inbound policy.
questions.distractor_summary: Zone authorization isn't reset, the firewall range doesn't explain the missing Google-internal answers, and Private Google Access is unrelated to DNS.

questions.question: VMs in a VPC call a partner API at `api.partner.com`. During a migration, the company must temporarily make VMs in this VPC resolve only `api.partner.com` to a private IP reached over Interconnect, while all other `partner.com` names resolve publicly. The company doesn't own `partner.com`. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a private zone for `partner.com` that contains only `api.partner.com` for the application.
Use a DNS peering zone for `partner.com` into the partner's network.
Use a forwarding zone for `partner.com` to the on-premises DNS servers across the subscriptions.
Use a response policy on the VPC with a rule for `api.partner.com` returning the private IP.
questions.correct_rationale: Response policy rules can override the answer for a specific name while all other names resolve normally.
questions.distractor_summary: A private zone for `partner.com` would make all other `partner.com` names fail to resolve, and peering or forwarding the whole domain changes resolution for every name, not just one.

questions.question: A platform team wants DNS records in a Cloud DNS public zone to be created and updated automatically whenever developers deploy Kubernetes Services and Ingresses in GKE. The team wants to avoid long-lived service account keys. What should the engineer implement?
options: Use a Cloud Scheduler job that updates the records from `kubectl` output across the subscriptions.
Use Cloud DNS routing policies that are linked to the GKE cluster.
Use ExternalDNS in the cluster with Workload Identity Federation for GKE and `roles/dns.admin`.
Use a DNS peering zone from the cluster's VPC to the public zone.
questions.correct_rationale: ExternalDNS watches Services and Ingresses and manages Cloud DNS records, and Workload Identity Federation for GKE provides credentials without keys.
questions.distractor_summary: A scheduled script adds delay and custom code, routing policies don't create records from Kubernetes objects, and DNS peering affects resolution rather than record management.

questions.question: An internal application is served by internal passthrough Network Load Balancers in `us-east1` (primary) and `us-west1` (backup). Clients resolve `app.internal.example.com` from a Cloud DNS private zone. The company wants DNS to return the backup load balancer automatically if the primary's backends become unhealthy. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a weighted round robin routing policy with 100 and 0 weights for the two regions for the application.
Use a failover routing policy with health checking, naming the primary and backup LB forwarding rules.
Use two A records with the same name and a low TTL for the two load balancers throughout the organization.
Use a geolocation routing policy that maps each region to its own load balancer across the subscriptions.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud DNS failover routing policies with health checks return the backup target when the primary internal load balancer's backends are unhealthy.
questions.distractor_summary: Static weights don't react to health, multiple A records return both addresses to clients regardless of health, and geolocation routing picks by client location rather than failing over.

questions.question: A security team investigating possible malware on VMs wants to review every DNS query made by VMs in a production VPC, including queries answered from private zones. What should the engineer enable?
options: Use Cloud DNS logging through a DNS server policy on the VPC with logging turned on.
Use VPC Flow Logs on all subnets with the metadata included in each of the records overall.
Use Firewall Rules Logging on the implied egress rule for all of the VMs.
Use Data Access audit logs for the Cloud DNS API to review each of the queries.
questions.correct_rationale: Enabling logging in a DNS server policy records queries resolved by Cloud DNS for VMs in the attached VPC, including private zone answers.
questions.distractor_summary: VPC Flow Logs don't capture queries to the metadata-server resolver, implied rules can't be logged, and Data Access audit logs record API calls rather than name resolution.

questions.question: A company's VMs without external IPs call a partner's API, and the partner allowlists source IPs. The Cloud NAT gateway uses automatic IP allocation, and after scaling events the partner sees traffic from new, unapproved IPs. What should the engineer do?
options: Assign a static external IP address to each of the VMs for the partner calls.
Use Private NAT for the partner traffic that leaves the VPC for their network.
Increase the minimum ports per VM so that fewer NAT IP addresses are needed.
Reserve static external IPs, use Cloud NAT manual IP allocation, and share them with the partner.
questions.correct_rationale: Manual NAT IP allocation uses only reserved addresses, so the set of source IPs is predictable and can be allowlisted.
questions.distractor_summary: Per-VM external IPs remove the benefits of NAT and expose VMs, Private NAT is for private destinations, and port tuning doesn't guarantee automatic allocation won't add addresses.

questions.question: A Cloud NAT gateway serves VMs with widely varying connection counts. The engineer tries to enable dynamic port allocation so busy VMs receive more ports, but the update fails. The gateway has endpoint-independent mapping enabled. What should the engineer do?
options: Switch to manual NAT IP allocation first and then change the port settings.
Delete the gateway and create a Private NAT gateway in its place for the VMs.
Disable endpoint-independent mapping, then enable dynamic port allocation with minimum and maximum ports.
Set the minimum ports per VM to 65,536 so that every VM has enough ports.
questions.correct_rationale: Dynamic port allocation isn't compatible with endpoint-independent mapping, so EIM must be disabled before enabling DPA. Manual IP allocation works with DPA but doesn't resolve the conflict, Private NAT serves a different use case, and 65,536 exceeds the maximum ports per VM.

questions.question: Application VMs behind Cloud NAT hold long-lived connections to an external database that can be idle for 30 minutes between queries. Applications report that connections are reset after about 20 minutes of inactivity. The external database's settings aren't the cause. What should the engineer do?
options: Raise the Cloud NAT TCP idle timeout above 30 minutes, or use shorter TCP keepalives.
Increase the minimum ports per VM for the long-lived database connections.
Switch Cloud NAT to automatic IP allocation for the VMs that hold the connections.
Enable endpoint-independent mapping so that idle connections are not dropped.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud NAT's default established TCP idle timeout is 1,200 seconds (20 minutes), after which idle mappings are removed; raising the timeout or using keepalives keeps connections open.
questions.distractor_summary: Port counts, IP allocation, and EIM don't affect idle timeouts.

questions.question: A central security team wants to ensure that only designated subnets in approved projects can use Cloud NAT across the organization, preventing teams from creating NAT gateways that give internet egress to sensitive subnets. What should the engineer implement?
options: Use an IAM deny policy that blocks `compute.routers.create` in all of the projects.
Use the organization policy `constraints/compute.restrictCloudNATUsage` to list the allowed subnets.
Use a hierarchical firewall policy that denies egress to `0.0.0.0/0` for the workloads.
Use the organization policy constraint `constraints/compute.vmExternalIpAccess` on the projects overall.
questions.correct_rationale: The `restrictCloudNATUsage` constraint defines which subnets are allowed to use Cloud NAT. Denying Cloud Router creation blocks legitimate hybrid routing, a blanket egress deny also blocks approved subnets, and `vmExternalIpAccess` controls external IPs on VMs rather than NAT.

questions.question: A regulated company requires that workloads access the internet only through an explicit proxy that enforces URL-level policies (for example, allowing only specific GitHub repository paths), inspects TLS, and logs every request with the calling workload's identity. It prefers a managed Google Cloud service. What should the engineer deploy?
options: Use Cloud NAT with endpoint-independent mapping and logging for the internet access.
Use Cloud Armor edge security policies on an external load balancer for the egress.
Use egress firewall rules with FQDN objects for `github.com` for the egress traffic.
Use Secure Web Proxy with URL-list policies, TLS inspection and Cloud Logging.
questions.correct_rationale: Secure Web Proxy is a managed explicit proxy that enforces URL- and identity-based policies on egress web traffic, supports TLS inspection, and logs requests.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud NAT translates addresses without filtering, Cloud Armor protects inbound traffic to load balancers, and FQDN firewall objects work at the domain level and can't match URL paths.

questions.question: A company's VMs use one Cloud NAT gateway. Traffic to a partner at `203.0.113.0/24` must come from a specific allowlisted NAT IP, while all other internet traffic should use the gateway's general NAT IP pool. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use two Cloud NAT gateways on the same Cloud Router for the same subnets.
Use tag-based routes that send the partner traffic through a separate NAT VM.
Use a Cloud NAT rule for destination `203.0.113.0/24` with the dedicated NAT IP, default pool otherwise.
Use Private NAT for the partner destination so that the address is translated.
questions.correct_rationale: Public Cloud NAT rules can select specific NAT IPs based on destination, so partner traffic uses the allowlisted address while other traffic uses the default pool.
questions.distractor_summary: A subnet range can be served by only one NAT gateway, self-managed NAT VMs add operational overhead, and Private NAT is for private networks rather than internet destinations.

questions.question: Some batch VMs behind Cloud NAT intermittently fail to open outbound connections during peak processing, while other VMs work normally. The engineer suspects NAT port exhaustion but needs evidence before changing the configuration. What should the engineer do first?
options: Enable VPC Flow Logs with 100% sampling on the subnet of the batch VMs.
Enable Cloud NAT error logging and look for `OUT_OF_RESOURCES` drops, plus NAT allocation-failed metrics.
Enable Firewall Rules Logging on all of the egress rules of the VPC network.
Run Connectivity Tests from a batch VM to the internet to find the failures.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud NAT error logs record connections dropped because of port exhaustion with the `OUT_OF_RESOURCES` reason, and Cloud Monitoring exposes NAT allocation-failure metrics per VM. Flow logs and firewall logs don't show NAT port allocation, and Connectivity Tests analyze configuration rather than runtime port usage.

questions.question: A firewall appliance VM has `nic0` in `untrust-vpc` and `nic1` in `trust-vpc`. Traffic from `trust-vpc` clients reaches the appliance on `nic1`, but replies to clients in a different `trust-vpc` subnet leave via `nic0` and are dropped. What should the engineer do?
options: Use policy-based routing in the guest OS so `trust-vpc` ranges are sent out `nic1` to its gateway.
Swap `nic0` and `nic1` on the running VM so that the interfaces change roles.
Enable Private Google Access on `trust-vpc` so that the appliance can reply to it for the application.
Create a VPC route in `trust-vpc` that points to `nic0` of the appliance.
questions.correct_rationale: By default, only `nic0` receives a default gateway in the guest OS, so traffic to non-local subnets exits through it unless guest routing directs the `trust-vpc` ranges to `nic1`. NIC order can't be swapped on an existing VM, Private Google Access is unrelated, and VPC routes in `trust-vpc` can't point to an interface that lives in another VPC.

questions.question: A company must inspect all traffic between `spoke-a-vpc` and `spoke-b-vpc` with third-party firewall appliances. Peering or NCC between the spokes isn't allowed, because all traffic must flow through the appliances. What design meets the requirement?
options: Peer both spokes to a hub VPC with the appliances and rely on peering route exchange across the subscriptions.
Deploy the appliances with Cloud NAT in each of the spoke VPCs for the traffic.
Use Cloud NGFW Enterprise endpoints in each spoke and join the spokes with an NCC mesh for the application.
Use multi-NIC appliances with a NIC in each spoke, each behind an internal NLB with routes in each spoke.
questions.correct_rationale: Multi-NIC appliances bridge the VPCs, and an internal load balancer next hop in each spoke forces inter-spoke traffic through them with health-checked high availability.
questions.distractor_summary: Peering to a hub isn't transitive, Cloud NAT doesn't route between VPCs, and connecting the spokes directly with NCC violates the requirement even if NGFW is added.

questions.question: A company runs firewall appliances that must survive a zone failure and automatically replace failed instances. Appliance VMs are created from an instance template. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use a zonal unmanaged instance group behind an internal load balancer for the appliances for the team.
Use two standalone VMs with static routes of different priorities for the appliances in every region.
Use a regional MIG with IP forwarding, autohealing and an internal passthrough NLB as the next hop.
Use a single large VM with a live migration policy to keep the appliance running for the application.
questions.correct_rationale: A regional MIG spreads appliances across zones and autoheals failed instances, IP forwarding lets them route transit traffic, and an internal load balancer next hop sends traffic only to healthy appliances.
questions.distractor_summary: Zonal or unmanaged groups don't survive zone failures or autoheal, static-route failover doesn't detect software failures, and a single VM is a single point of failure.

questions.question: A security team needs a third-party intrusion detection system to receive copies of traffic to and from database VMs in `us-central1`. They want to minimize the volume of mirrored traffic and cost. What should the engineer configure?
options: Use VPC Flow Logs with 100% sampling that are exported to the IDS for analysis.
Use a Packet Mirroring policy with the database VMs as sources and an internal passthrough collector LB.
Use a policy-based route that sends the database traffic through the IDS VMs.
Use a Packet Mirroring policy with an external passthrough NLB collector in another region.
questions.correct_rationale: Packet Mirroring clones traffic to a collector internal load balancer in the same region, and filters by protocol, CIDR, and direction reduce mirrored volume and cost.
questions.distractor_summary: Flow logs contain metadata rather than payloads, inline routing makes the IDS a point of failure, and collectors must be internal load balancers in the same region.

questions.question: A company deployed Cloud IDS and receives alerts about exploit attempts against its web VMs. Management now requires that malicious traffic be blocked in-line automatically, using a Google-managed service rather than third-party appliances. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Deploy Cloud NGFW Enterprise with intrusion prevention profiles applied by firewall policy rules.
Change the Cloud IDS endpoint severity setting to block mode for the web VMs across the subscriptions.
Increase Packet Mirroring coverage to all of the VMs in the project's VPC across the subscriptions.
Create Cloud Armor rules from the Cloud IDS alerts for the web VMs.
questions.correct_rationale: Cloud IDS is detection-only using mirrored traffic, while Cloud NGFW Enterprise provides in-line intrusion prevention that can block threats.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud IDS has no block mode, more mirroring still only detects, and Cloud Armor protects load balancer backends rather than filtering traffic to VMs directly.

questions.question: A company ordered a Dedicated Interconnect connection in a colocation facility where it already has routers. Google has emailed the Letter of Authorization and Connecting Facility Assignment (LOA-CFA). The project manager asks what the next step is. What should the network engineer do?
options: Create VLAN attachments and Cloud Routers right away, then wait for Google to install the circuit overall.
Send the LOA-CFA to Google Cloud Support so that they activate the connection.
Give the LOA-CFA to the colo provider for the cross-connect, then wait for Google's circuit tests.
Configure BGP on the on-premises router with Google's public ASN before the tests.
questions.correct_rationale: The LOA-CFA authorizes the colocation provider to install the cross-connect to Google's equipment; after that, Google tests the circuit before VLAN attachments are created.
questions.distractor_summary: VLAN attachments can't pass traffic until the circuit is provisioned, Google Support doesn't install cross-connects, and BGP is configured per VLAN attachment later using the Cloud Router's ASN.

questions.question: A new single-circuit 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect passed Google's light-level tests, but the link never comes up after the company connects its router. The router port is configured with a 10GBASE-LR optic and a plain routed interface with no port-channel. What is the most likely issue?
options: Dedicated Interconnect requires LACP, even for a single circuit, so the port must be in an LACP bundle.
Single circuits require 100GBASE-LR4 optics on the router that connects to Google.
The router must use multimode fiber for the Dedicated Interconnect circuit to Google.
The router must first establish an IPsec tunnel with Google over the circuit.
questions.correct_rationale: Google requires LACP on Dedicated Interconnect connections regardless of circuit count, so the port must be part of a link aggregation group. 10GBASE-LR over single-mode fiber is correct for a 10 Gbps circuit, multimode fiber isn't supported, and IPsec isn't part of bringing up the physical link.

questions.question: A company's single 10 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connection, carrying one VLAN attachment, is consistently saturated at peak. The company expects to need about 30 Gbps within a year and wants to keep the same colocation facility and edge availability domain for this connection (redundancy is handled by a separate connection). What should the engineer do?
options: Create additional VLAN attachments on the same 10 Gbps circuit to add capacity.
Replace the connection with Partner Interconnect at 50 Gbps for the extra capacity in every region.
Add HA VPN tunnels and use ECMP together with the Interconnect for the capacity for the application.
Add circuits to the connection's bundle, such as 4×10 Gbps, and increase the attachment capacity.
questions.correct_rationale: A Dedicated Interconnect connection can bundle multiple 10 Gbps circuits in one LACP group, and VLAN attachment capacity can be increased to use the added bandwidth.
questions.distractor_summary: More attachments on the same circuit share its 10 Gbps, Partner Interconnect adds provider dependency without being necessary, and internet VPN tunnels add limited, lower-quality capacity.

questions.question: A company buys Partner Interconnect from a Layer 2 service provider. After the provider activates the VLAN attachments, no routes are exchanged between the company's data center and Google Cloud. Who is responsible for configuring BGP?
options: The service provider, who sets up BGP between its own routers and Cloud Router.
The company, who sets up BGP sessions between its on-premises router and Cloud Router.
Google, who sets up the BGP sessions automatically once the attachment is activated overall.
No one, since Layer 2 Partner Interconnect uses static routes only for the traffic.
questions.correct_rationale: With Layer 2 Partner Interconnect, the provider delivers a Layer 2 path, and the customer configures BGP between its own router and Cloud Router.
questions.distractor_summary: With Layer 3 partners, the provider handles the BGP session with Cloud Router, which is a key distinction on the exam.

questions.question: A network engineer is provisioning Partner Interconnect for the first time. The service provider's portal asks for a key to connect the company's circuit to Google Cloud. What is the correct sequence?
options: Create a `PARTNER` VLAN attachment with a Cloud Router, get the pairing key and give it to the provider.
Order the connection in the provider's portal and give the LOA-CFA from Google to the provider.
Create a Dedicated Interconnect order, then convert it to a Partner Interconnect one.
Create an HA VPN gateway, share its IP with the provider, and let it create the attachment.
questions.correct_rationale: Partner Interconnect provisioning starts in Google Cloud by creating a Partner VLAN attachment, which generates a pairing key for the provider, followed by activation.
questions.distractor_summary: LOA-CFAs are part of Dedicated Interconnect, the order types can't be converted, and HA VPN is a separate product.

questions.question: A bank's two 100 Gbps Dedicated Interconnect connections carry high-volume database replication. A new policy requires encryption of all traffic on these links, but the IPsec throughput and CPU overhead on the bank's edge routers are unacceptable at these speeds. The routers support hardware MACsec. What should the engineer implement?
options: Use HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect with multiple tunnels for the replication throughout the organization.
Use TLS on the replication application only, with the Interconnect left as it is across the subscriptions.
Use MACsec for Cloud Interconnect on both connections, with keys on the Interconnect and the routers.
Migrate to Partner Interconnect with a provider that encrypts the traffic for the bank in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: MACsec provides line-rate Layer 2 encryption between on-premises routers and Google's edge on Dedicated Interconnect, avoiding IPsec overhead.
questions.distractor_summary: HA VPN over Interconnect adds the IPsec overhead the bank wants to avoid, application TLS doesn't cover all traffic, and moving to Partner Interconnect doesn't guarantee link encryption.

questions.question: A company's VPC and on-premises storage network both use jumbo frames with a 8,896-byte MTU. Over Dedicated Interconnect, large storage replication transfers perform poorly and packet captures show fragmentation. The VLAN attachment was created with default settings. What should the engineer change?
options: Enable Path MTU Discovery on Cloud Router for the VLAN attachments of the link overall.
Lower the VPC MTU to 1,300 bytes so that the packets fit in the tunnel.
Add a second VLAN attachment so that the traffic is split between the attachments.
Set the VLAN attachment MTU to 8,896 bytes to match the VPC and on-premises MTU.
questions.correct_rationale: VLAN attachments support configurable MTUs, including 8,896 bytes, and should match the VPC and on-premises MTU to avoid fragmentation.
questions.distractor_summary: Cloud Router doesn't handle the data plane, lowering the VPC MTU sacrifices performance, and more attachments don't change per-packet MTU.

questions.question: A company's physical Dedicated Interconnect connections are owned by an `infra-interconnect` project for billing and administration. Its Shared VPC network is in a separate `net-host` project. How should the engineer connect the Shared VPC to on-premises?
options: Move the Interconnect connections to the `net-host` project for the attachments.
Create the VLAN attachments and Cloud Routers in `net-host`, using the connections from `infra-interconnect`.
Create the VLAN attachments in `infra-interconnect` and peer its VPC with the Shared VPC across the subscriptions.
Create an HA VPN from `infra-interconnect` to `net-host` over the Interconnect.
questions.correct_rationale: Dedicated Interconnect connections can be used by VLAN attachments in other projects, so attachments and Cloud Routers belong in the host project that owns the VPC. Moving connections is unnecessary, peering doesn't carry dynamic routes to on-premises transitively without extra configuration and adds a hop, and a VPN over the Interconnect adds needless complexity.

questions.question: A company transfers about 200 TB per month from Google Cloud to its data center for backup and analytics, currently over HA VPN across the internet. Finance wants to reduce the cost of this traffic, and networking wants more consistent throughput. What should the engineer recommend?
options: Use Cloud Interconnect, since its egress is priced lower than internet egress and bandwidth is dedicated.
Use Premium Tier networking for the VPN gateway IP addresses of the data center.
Increase the number of the HA VPN tunnels to carry the larger transfers.
Use Cloud CDN in front of the storage buckets to lower the transfer costs.
questions.correct_rationale: Data transfer out through Cloud Interconnect has lower per-GB pricing than internet egress, and dedicated capacity provides consistent throughput, which justifies Interconnect at high volumes.
questions.distractor_summary: Premium Tier doesn't lower costs, more VPN tunnels still use internet egress pricing, and Cloud CDN caches content for end users rather than bulk backup transfers.

questions.question: A company has redundant Dedicated Interconnect connections in edge availability domains `zone1` and `zone2` in one metro. Google sends a planned maintenance notice for `zone1`. What should the engineer do to prepare?
options: Open a support case to postpone the maintenance of the `zone1` connections.
Delete the `zone1` VLAN attachments before the start of the maintenance window in every region.
Check that `zone2` has capacity and learns and advertises the same routes so BGP fails over.
Create an HA VPN backup for the duration of the maintenance of the connections in every region.
questions.correct_rationale: Google performs maintenance on one edge availability domain at a time so that redundant designs keep running, and the engineer should confirm the other domain can carry the load with matching routes.
questions.distractor_summary: Maintenance generally can't be postponed, deleting attachments causes unnecessary reconfiguration, and a VPN backup isn't needed if the redundant design is healthy.

questions.question: A branch office has a single VPN device with one public IP address. The company wants the 99.99% availability SLA on the Google Cloud side of the HA VPN connection. How should the tunnels be configured?
options: Use one tunnel from interface 0 of the HA VPN gateway to the peer IP address.
Use two Classic VPN tunnels to the peer IP address from the gateway.
Use two HA VPN gateways, each with one tunnel to the peer IP address.
Use one tunnel from each HA VPN interface to the peer's single IP, each with its own BGP session.
questions.correct_rationale: Google's HA VPN SLA on its side requires tunnels from both gateway interfaces, which can terminate on a single peer IP; the peer device remains a single point of failure outside Google's SLA. A single tunnel doesn't qualify, Classic VPN has a lower SLA, and two gateways with one tunnel each don't form the supported topology.

questions.question: A company uses a policy-based Classic VPN to a legacy firewall. The tunnel shows as established, and traffic from `10.1.0.0/24` flows, but traffic from a newly added subnet `10.1.1.0/24` never reaches on-premises. The firewall's local and remote traffic selectors weren't changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: Classic VPN supports only one subnet for each tunnel of the policy-based VPN throughout the organization.
The new subnet is missing from the traffic selectors on one or both sides, so the IPsec SA excludes it.
The VPC is in regional dynamic routing mode, which blocks the policy-based tunnels.
The new subnet requires Private Google Access before it can use the tunnel.
questions.correct_rationale: With policy-based VPN, traffic selectors define which source and destination ranges are protected, and they must match on both sides, so a new subnet must be added to both.
questions.distractor_summary: Classic VPN can include multiple ranges, dynamic routing mode affects BGP routes rather than policy-based tunnels, and Private Google Access is unrelated.

questions.question: A company needs about 10 Gbps of encrypted connectivity to Google Cloud over the internet while it waits several months for Interconnect. A single HA VPN tunnel pair isn't delivering enough throughput. What should the engineer do?
options: Increase the MTU on the VPN tunnels to 8,896 bytes to carry more traffic.
Switch to Classic VPN, which has a higher throughput for each of the tunnels.
Add more HA VPN tunnels with BGP sessions of equal priority so ECMP distributes the traffic.
Enable Premium Tier on the VPC so that the VPN tunnels carry more traffic.
